lessons.title: Letters and Sounds
lessons.content:
# Letters and Sounds

English is written with 26 letters, but it is spoken with about 44 different sounds. This is why spelling alone cannot tell you how a word is said. The letter a stands for a different sound in cat, car, cake and about.

Speech sounds fall into two groups. Vowels are made with the air flowing freely through the mouth, with no blockage. Consonants are made when the air is stopped or squeezed somewhere in the mouth or throat. Standard British English has about 20 vowel sounds (12 pure vowels and 8 diphthongs) and 24 consonant sounds.

Dictionaries show pronunciation with special symbols called phonetic symbols, written between slanted lines, for example /kæt/ for cat. A colon after a vowel, as in /i:/, shows that the vowel is long.

Class activity: say these pairs aloud and decide whether the vowel is the same or different: bed/bad, seat/sit, cot/caught.

quiz.question: About how many sounds does spoken English have?
What does the colon in /i:/ show?

lessons.title: The Vowels /i:/ and /ɪ/
lessons.content:
# The Vowels /i:/ and /ɪ/

The vowel /i:/ is long. Your lips are spread as in a smile and the tongue stays high and forward. It is the sound in see, team, receive and people. The vowel /ɪ/ is short and more relaxed, as in sit, bit, women and busy.

Pairs that differ only in these two vowels: seat/sit, leave/live, feel/fill, heat/hit, sheep/ship, beat/bit. A wrong vowel can change the word entirely: Please do not slip on the sheep is not the same sentence as Please do not slip on the ship.

Practice sentences: The green team will reach the field. Is this a big fish in the dish? Read each sentence slowly, then at normal speed, holding /i:/ a little longer than /ɪ/.

quiz.question: Which word contains /i:/?
Which pair differs only by /i:/ and /ɪ/?

lessons.title: The Vowels /e/ and /æ/
lessons.content:
# The Vowels /e/ and /æ/

The vowel /e/ is the middle sound in pen, bed, head and said. The mouth is half open. The vowel /æ/ needs a wider mouth, with the jaw lowered, as in pan, bad, cat and hand.

Pairs: pen/pan, men/man, bed/bad, set/sat, pet/pat, said/sad, bend/band. Many learners say both vowels the same, so that men and man sound alike. Open your mouth wider for /æ/ and check the difference in a mirror.

Practice sentences: Ten men sat on the red bench. The bad man had a sad hand. Notice that the letter a stands for /æ/ in hand and for a different sound in father.

Which pair differs only by /e/ and /æ/?

lessons.title: The Vowels /ɑ:/ and /ʌ/
lessons.content:
# The Vowels /ɑ:/ and /ʌ/

The vowel /ɑ:/ is long and made at the back of the mouth with the mouth wide open. It is heard in car, farm, father, heart and calm. The vowel /ʌ/ is short, as in cup, bus, love, come and blood.

Pairs: cart/cut, park/puck, heart/hut, march/much, dark/duck, bark/buck. Say the first word of each pair with a wide, open mouth, and the second with a short, relaxed vowel.

Note the spelling traps. The letter o is /ʌ/ in love, come, money and son. The letters ear is /ɑ:/ in heart. Always check a dictionary when a word looks unfamiliar.

lessons.title: The Vowels /ɒ/ and /ɔ:/
lessons.content:
# The Vowels /ɒ/ and /ɔ:/

The vowel /ɒ/ is short, with rounded lips and a low tongue, as in pot, hot, dog, and watch. The vowel /ɔ:/ is long and lips are more rounded, as in port, short, door, and law.

Pairs: pot/port, cot/caught, shot/short, not/nought, stock/stork. Many Nigerian speakers use a single rounded vowel for both. Listen for the length: /ɔ:/ is held about twice as long as /ɒ/.

Practice: The hot dog is on the long walk to the shop. A short man bought a lot of corn.

lessons.title: The Vowels /ʊ/ and /u:/
lessons.content:
# The Vowels /ʊ/ and /u:/

The vowel /ʊ/ is short and relaxed, as in put, book, good and full. The vowel /u:/ is long with tightly rounded lips, as in food, blue, group, and too.

Pairs: full/fool, pull/pool, look/Luke, wood/who'd. The words book and food are spelt with oo but do not share a vowel.

Practice: The cook took a good look at the book. Two new boots are in the blue room.

lessons.title: The Vowels /ɜ:/ and /ə/
lessons.content:
# The Vowels /ɜ:/ and /ə/

The vowel /ɜ:/ is long and made with the tongue in the middle of the mouth, as in bird, work, learn, and turn. Notice that bird, work and learn are spelt with different letters but share one sound.

The vowel /ə/ is called schwa. It is the most common vowel in English, and is always short and weak. It occurs in unstressed syllables: about, teacher, doctor, banana (/bəˈnɑːnə/).

Practice: The girl learnt to work with a third teacher. Mark the schwa in the words: sister, today, family, police.

Which word contains /ɜ:/?

lessons.title: Diphthongs
lessons.content:
# Diphthongs

A diphthong is a vowel sound that glides from one vowel position to another within one syllable. Standard English has eight: /eɪ/ as in day, /aɪ/ as in high, /ɔɪ/ as in boy, /əʊ/ as in go, /aʊ/ as in now, /ɪə/ as in here, /eə/ as in hair, and /ʊə/ as in tour.

Pairs worth practising: late/let, bite/bit, boat/bought, now/no. Hold the first part of the sound and glide smoothly to the second part.

Practice: Tell the boy to go home today. How now, brown cow?

quiz.question: How many diphthongs are in standard British English?
Which word contains /aɪ/?

lessons.title: Consonant Contrasts: /p/ /b/, /t/ /d/, /θ/ /ð/
lessons.content:
# Consonant Contrasts: /p/ /b/, /t/ /d/, /θ/ /ð/

Voiceless consonants are made without vibration in the throat; voiced ones are made with it. Place a finger on your throat and say /s/ then /z/ to feel the difference. The pairs /p/ and /b/, /t/ and /d/, /θ/ and /ð/ differ only in voicing.

The sound /θ/ is voiceless, as in think, three and bath. The sound /ð/ is voiced, as in this, mother and breathe. To make them, place the tip of the tongue lightly between the teeth. Many learners replace them with /t/ and /d/, so that think sounds like tink.

Practice: Those three thin brothers think that this is the other path.

lessons.title: Nouns
lessons.content:
# Nouns

A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. Common nouns name general things: girl, market, river. Proper nouns name particular people or places and begin with capital letters: Amina, Ibadan, River Niger. Abstract nouns name things we cannot touch: honesty, freedom, hunger. Collective nouns name groups: a class of pupils, a flock of birds, a team of players.

Countable nouns can be numbered (one book, three books). Uncountable nouns cannot (water, rice, advice), so we say some rice, not a rice. Practice: Sort these into common and proper: Lagos, city, teacher, Mr Bello.

Which is a collective noun?

lessons.title: Pronouns
lessons.content:
# Pronouns

A pronoun takes the place of a noun so we do not repeat it. Personal pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they (subject) and me, him, her, us, them (object). Possessive pronouns show ownership: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves: myself, himself, themselves.

Example: Tunde lost his pen, so Ada gave him hers. Practice: Replace the nouns with pronouns: Ngozi told Ngozi's brother that Ngozi would help the boys.

quiz.question: Which is a possessive pronoun?
Choose the reflexive pronoun: The boy hurt ____.

lessons.title: Verbs
lessons.content:
# Verbs

A verb shows an action or a state. Action verbs: run, write, cook. State or linking verbs join the subject to more information: be, seem, become (She is a nurse. He seems tired). Auxiliary or helping verbs support the main verb: is, are, was, have, will, can (They are playing).

Regular verbs add -ed in the past (walk, walked). Irregular verbs change form (go, went; write, wrote; eat, ate). Practice: Underline the verb in each sentence: The market opens early. Chidi has finished his work.

lessons.title: Simple Tenses
lessons.content:
# Simple Tenses

Tense tells us when something happens. The simple present states habits and facts: She sells bread every morning. The simple past tells of finished actions: She sold bread yesterday. The simple future uses will: She will sell bread tomorrow.

Third person singular subjects take -s in the present: he walks, she goes, it works. Practice: Put into the simple past: We eat rice on Sundays. Put into the future: The teacher marks our books.

quiz.question: Which sentence is in the simple past?
Fill in: The sun ____ in the east.

lessons.title: Adjectives and Comparison
lessons.content:
# Adjectives and Comparison

Adjectives describe nouns: a tall tree, three red cars. Most adjectives have three degrees. Positive: tall. Comparative: taller (compares two things). Superlative: tallest (compares three or more). Short adjectives add -er and -est. Longer ones use more and most: more beautiful, most beautiful.

Some are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst. Practice: Complete: Ife is ____ than Bola (tall). Of the three, this road is the ____ (bad).

lessons.title: Adverbs
lessons.content:
# Adverbs

An adverb tells us more about a verb, an adjective or another adverb. Adverbs of manner say how: slowly, carefully. Adverbs of time say when: yesterday, soon. Adverbs of place say where: here, outside. Many adverbs of manner are formed by adding -ly to an adjective: quick, quickly.

Examples: The girl sang beautifully. He arrived late. Practice: Pick the adverb: The driver stopped suddenly near the school.

lessons.title: Prepositions and Conjunctions
lessons.content:
# Prepositions and Conjunctions

Prepositions show the relationship between a noun and another word, often position or time: on the table, under the tree, at six o'clock, in June, between two houses.

Conjunctions join words or sentences: and, but, or, because, although, so. Example: I wanted to go, but it rained. Practice: Fill in: The book is ____ the desk. She was late ____ the bus broke down.

quiz.question: Which is a preposition?
Choose the conjunction: 'He is rich but unhappy.'

lessons.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
lessons.content:
# Subject-Verb Agreement

The verb must agree with its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb: The boy runs. A plural subject takes a plural verb: The boys run. Words like everybody, each and none take singular verbs: Each of the girls has a book.

When the subject is two nouns joined by and, the verb is plural: Musa and Ali are friends. Practice: Choose the correct verb: The team (is, are) ready. My brothers (plays, play) football.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
Fill in: Each of the boys ____ a pen.

lessons.title: Punctuation and Capital Letters
lessons.content:
# Punctuation and Capital Letters

Begin every sentence, name, day, month and place name with a capital letter. End statements with a full stop, questions with a question mark and exclamations with an exclamation mark. Use a comma to separate items in a list: We bought rice, beans, yam and oil.

An apostrophe shows ownership (the girl's bag) or a missing letter (don't = do not). Quotation marks enclose direct speech: Ada said, "I am ready." Practice: Punctuate: where is tunde asked the teacher

lessons.title: Reading for Meaning
lessons.content:
# Reading for Meaning

Good readers use different strategies. Skimming means glancing quickly over a text to get the general idea. Scanning means searching for a specific detail, like a date or name. Careful reading means reading slowly to understand the full meaning.

After reading a passage, find the main idea (what the whole passage is mostly about) and supporting details (facts that explain it). Practice: Read a short newspaper report and write one sentence stating its main idea.

lessons.title: Vocabulary from Context
lessons.content:
# Vocabulary from Context

When you meet a new word, look at the words around it for clues. Example: The weather was so inclement that the match was cancelled. The cancelled match suggests inclement means bad or stormy.

Also use word parts: un- means not (unhappy), re- means again (rewrite), -ful means full of (careful). Practice: Guess the meaning: The traders were jubilant when prices fell and sales rose.

quiz.question: The prefix un- means:
Context clues are found in:
options: the words around a new word

lessons.title: Writing a Paragraph
lessons.content:
# Writing a Paragraph

A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea. It usually has a topic sentence stating the main idea, supporting sentences giving details or examples, and a concluding sentence. Start the first line a little to the right (indentation) or leave a line between paragraphs.

Example topic sentence: Regular exercise keeps the body healthy. Supporting sentences might mention the heart, sleep and energy. Practice: Write a five-sentence paragraph on My School Library.

lessons.title: Descriptive Writing
lessons.content:
# Descriptive Writing

Descriptive writing paints a picture with words using the five senses: sight, sound, smell, taste and touch. Use specific adjectives and strong verbs rather than vague ones. Instead of The market was noisy, write Traders shouted prices over the roar of generators while the smell of fried plantain drifted between the stalls.

Plan by choosing a place or person, listing details for each sense, then arranging them in order, such as left to right. Practice: Describe your classroom in one paragraph.

lessons.title: Narrative Writing
lessons.content:
# Narrative Writing

A narrative tells a story. It has a beginning (characters and setting are introduced), a middle (a problem or conflict develops, reaching a climax) and an end (the problem is resolved). Narratives are usually in the past tense and may include dialogue.

Plan with the questions: Who? Where? What happened? How did it end? Practice: Write a story titled The Day the Power Came Back.

lessons.title: Informal Letters
lessons.content:
# Informal Letters

An informal or friendly letter is written to a relative or friend. Its parts are: the writer's address and date at the top right; the salutation (Dear Ngozi,); the body in paragraphs; the closing (Yours lovingly,) and the writer's name.

The tone is friendly and conversational, but spelling and grammar must still be correct. Practice: Write to a friend in another state describing your new school.

lessons.title: Introduction to Literature
lessons.content:
# Introduction to Literature

Literature in English is divided into three main genres. Prose is written in sentences and paragraphs: novels and short stories. Poetry is arranged in lines and stanzas, often with rhythm and imagery. Drama is written to be acted, with dialogue and stage directions.

Literature may be written or oral. Oral literature passes down by speaking, as with folktales and proverbs. Practice: Name one example of each genre you have read or seen.

lessons.title: Elements of Prose
lessons.content:
# Elements of Prose

Plot is the sequence of events. Characters are the people (or animals) in the story; the main character is the protagonist. Setting is the time and place. Theme is the central message, such as honesty or perseverance. The narrator is the voice telling the story.

When you read a story, ask: Who are the characters? Where and when does it happen? What problem arises? What lesson does it teach? Practice: Answer these questions about a story you know.

# Oral Literature: Folktales, Proverbs and Riddles

Nigeria has a rich oral tradition. Folktales are stories, often with animal characters, told to entertain and teach, such as the tortoise tales found across many communities. Proverbs are short wise sayings that carry a lesson. Riddles are puzzles that test thinking.

Oral literature is usually shared in the evening by elders. It teaches values like honesty, patience and respect. Practice: Ask an elder for a proverb in your language, write it down, translate it and explain its meaning.

lessons.title: Whole Numbers and Place Value
lessons.content:
# Whole Numbers and Place Value

Whole numbers are the counting numbers together with zero: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. We write them with ten digits, 0 to 9, and the value of a digit depends on its position. Reading from the right, the places are units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands and millions. Each place is worth ten times the place on its right.

Worked example 1: In 3,465,278 the digit 6 is in the ten-thousands place, so its value is 60,000. The digit 4 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 400,000.

Worked example 2: Write 3,465,278 in words. Three million, four hundred and sixty-five thousand, two hundred and seventy-eight.

Worked example 3: Write 2,000,000 + 300,000 + 40 as one number. Fill every empty place with zero: 2,300,040.

Practice: (a) State the value of 7 in 7,305,000. (b) Write 6,040,205 in words. (c) Write the number made of 5 millions, 3 thousands and 8 units.

lessons.title: Number Bases
lessons.content:
# Number Bases

Our everyday number system is base ten: it has ten digits and each place is worth ten times the one to its right. Other bases work the same way. In base two (binary) only the digits 0 and 1 are used and the places are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. Computers store all information in base two. In base five the digits are 0 to 4 and the places are 1, 5, 25, 125.

Worked example 1: Convert 1011 in base two to base ten. The places from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8. So 1011 = (1×8) + (0×4) + (1×2) + (1×1) = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.

Worked example 2: Convert 13 to base two. Divide repeatedly by 2 and record the remainders. 13 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 1; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1. Read the remainders upwards: 1101. Check: 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.

Worked example 3: Convert 29 to base five. 29 ÷ 5 = 5 remainder 4; 5 ÷ 5 = 1 remainder 0; 1 ÷ 5 = 0 remainder 1. Reading upwards gives 104 in base five. Check: 25 + 0 + 4 = 29.

Practice: (a) Convert 110 (base two) to base ten. (b) Convert 7 to base two. (c) Convert 243 (base five) to base ten.

lessons.title: Factors, Multiples and Prime Numbers
lessons.content:
# Factors, Multiples and Prime Numbers

A factor of a number divides it exactly with no remainder. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. A multiple of a number is what you get by multiplying it by 1, 2, 3 and so on. The multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and so on, without end.

A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. The primes below 20 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19. The number 2 is the only even prime. The number 1 is not prime because it has only one factor. A number with more than two factors is called composite.

Worked example: Write 60 as a product of prime factors. 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 2² × 3 × 5. A factor tree is a good way to do this: keep splitting each branch until every end is prime.

Practice: (a) List all factors of 18. (b) Write the first five multiples of 7. (c) Write 36 as a product of primes.

lessons.title: Highest Common Factor and Lowest Common Multiple
lessons.content:
# Highest Common Factor and Lowest Common Multiple

The highest common factor (HCF) of two or more numbers is the largest number that divides all of them exactly. The lowest common multiple (LCM) is the smallest number that is a multiple of all of them.

Worked example 1 (listing): Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, so the HCF is 6.

Worked example 2 (prime factors): 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3². For the HCF take the lowest power of each common prime: 2² × 3 = 12. For the LCM take the highest power of each prime: 2³ × 3² = 72. Check: HCF × LCM = 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36.

Worked example 3 (word problem): Two bells ring every 12 minutes and every 15 minutes. They ring together at 8:00 am. They next ring together after the LCM of 12 and 15, which is 60 minutes, so at 9:00 am.

Practice: (a) Find the HCF of 8 and 20. (b) Find the LCM of 6 and 8. (c) Three buses leave a park every 10, 15 and 20 minutes. After how many minutes do they leave together?

lessons.title: Fractions
lessons.content:
# Fractions

A fraction names part of a whole. In 3/4 the denominator 4 says the whole is cut into 4 equal parts and the numerator 3 says how many parts we have. Equivalent fractions have the same value: 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. To reduce a fraction to its lowest terms divide top and bottom by their HCF.

Adding and subtracting: first make the denominators the same. Worked example: 1/4 + 2/3. The LCM of 4 and 3 is 12, so 1/4 = 3/12 and 2/3 = 8/12. The sum is 11/12. Subtracting: 5/6 − 1/3 = 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2.

Multiplying: multiply the tops and the bottoms. 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2. Dividing: turn the second fraction upside down and multiply. 2/5 ÷ 4/5 = 2/5 × 5/4 = 10/20 = 1/2.

A mixed number combines a whole number and a fraction. To change 2 1/2 to an improper fraction: (2 × 2) + 1 = 5, so it is 5/2. To change 7/3 to a mixed number: 7 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 1, so 2 1/3.

Practice: (a) 3/4 + 1/8. (b) 7/10 − 2/5. (c) 3/5 × 1/2. (d) Change 17/5 to a mixed number.

lessons.title: Decimals
lessons.content:
# Decimals

A decimal uses a point to separate whole numbers from parts. The places after the point are tenths, hundredths, thousandths. So 3.45 means 3 units, 4 tenths and 5 hundredths. To compare decimals, line up the points: 0.7 is bigger than 0.65 because 0.70 > 0.65.

Adding and subtracting: line up the decimal points. 3.45 + 2.7 = 6.15. Multiplying: ignore the points, multiply, then place the point so the answer has as many decimal places as both numbers together. 0.3 × 0.4: 3 × 4 = 12, with two decimal places gives 0.12.

Dividing by a decimal: multiply both numbers by 10 (or 100) to make the divisor whole. 4.8 ÷ 0.6 becomes 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

Fractions and decimals: divide the top by the bottom. 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Going back, 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4.

Practice: (a) 0.5 + 0.25. (b) 0.2 × 0.3. (c) 7.2 ÷ 0.9. (d) Write 3/4 as a decimal.

lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.content:
# Percentages

Percent means per hundred. 25% means 25 out of 100, which is 25/100 = 1/4 = 0.25. To find a percentage of an amount, change it to a fraction or decimal and multiply.

Worked example 1: Find 15% of ₦2,000. 0.15 × 2,000 = ₦300.

Worked example 2: Express 18 out of 24 as a percentage. 18/24 × 100 = 75%.

Worked example 3 (increase): A trader raises the price of ₦5,000 by 10%. 10% of 5,000 = 500, so the new price is ₦5,500.

Worked example 4 (discount): A bag costing ₦3,500 has 20% off. 20% of 3,500 = 700, so the sale price is 3,500 − 700 = ₦2,800.

Practice: (a) 50% of 80. (b) Express 12 out of 48 as a percentage. (c) A phone costing ₦40,000 is reduced by 15%. Find the new price.

lessons.title: Approximation and Rounding
lessons.content:
# Approximation and Rounding

We round numbers to make them simpler. To round to a place value, look at the digit just after it: if it is 5 or more, round up; if it is 4 or less, leave the digit as it is.

Worked example 1: Round 4,687 to the nearest hundred. The hundreds digit is 6 and the next digit is 8, so round up: 4,700.

Worked example 2: Round 52,849 to the nearest thousand. The next digit after 2 is 8, so round up: 53,000.

Worked example 3: Round 3.746 to 2 decimal places. The third decimal digit is 6, so round up: 3.75.

Estimating helps check answers: 48 × 21 is about 50 × 20 = 1,000. The exact answer is 1,008, which is close.

Practice: (a) Round 6,349 to the nearest hundred. (b) Round 2.349 to 1 decimal place. (c) Estimate 39 × 61.

lessons.title: Ratio and Proportion
lessons.content:
# Ratio and Proportion

A ratio compares quantities of the same kind. The ratio 12 : 18 simplifies by dividing both by 6 to 2 : 3. The order matters: boys to girls as 2 : 3 is not the same as girls to boys.

Sharing in a ratio. Worked example: Share ₦6,000 between Ada and Bayo in the ratio 2 : 3. Total parts = 2 + 3 = 5. One part = 6,000 ÷ 5 = ₦1,200. Ada gets 2 × 1,200 = ₦2,400 and Bayo gets 3 × 1,200 = ₦3,600. Check: 2,400 + 3,600 = 6,000.

Direct proportion means that when one quantity increases, the other increases in the same ratio. If 5 exercise books cost ₦750, then one costs ₦150 and eight cost 8 × 150 = ₦1,200.

A rate compares different kinds of quantities. If a car travels 120 km in 2 hours, its speed is 120 ÷ 2 = 60 km per hour.

Practice: (a) Simplify 15 : 25. (b) Share 80 in the ratio 3 : 1. (c) If 4 pens cost ₦200, find the cost of 7 pens.

lessons.title: Directed Numbers
lessons.content:
# Directed Numbers

Directed numbers are numbers with a sign: positive numbers are above zero and negative numbers are below zero. On a number line, numbers to the right are bigger. So −2 is bigger than −7. Real life examples are temperature below freezing, a bank overdraft and heights below sea level.

Adding and subtracting: adding a positive moves right; adding a negative or subtracting a positive moves left. Worked examples: −3 + 5 = 2; 4 − 7 = −3; −2 − 5 = −7. Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: 6 − (−2) = 8.

Multiplying and dividing: same signs give a positive answer, different signs give a negative answer. (−3) × 4 = −12; (−3) × (−4) = 12; −12 ÷ 3 = −4; −20 ÷ (−5) = 4.

Worked example (temperature): The temperature at night is −4°C. By noon it rises by 9 degrees. New temperature = −4 + 9 = 5°C.

Practice: (a) −6 + 2. (b) 3 − 8. (c) (−5) × (−2). (d) −18 ÷ 6.

lessons.title: Algebraic Expressions
lessons.content:
# Algebraic Expressions

In algebra we use letters to stand for numbers we do not yet know or that can change. A term is a single part of an expression, such as 3x. In 3x, the number 3 is the coefficient and x is the variable. A number alone, such as 5, is a constant. The expression 3x + 5 has two terms.

Writing expressions from words: a number increased by 7 is n + 7. Twice a number minus 3 is 2n − 3. Five more than three times y is 3y + 5. If one book costs ₦b, then 5 books cost 5b naira. The perimeter of a square of side s is 4s.

We leave out the multiplication sign: 4 × a is written 4a, and a × b is written ab. A number multiplied by itself, a × a, is written a².

Worked example: A boy has x oranges. His sister has 3 more than he does. Together they have x + (x + 3) = 2x + 3 oranges.

Practice: (a) Write an expression for 5 less than y. (b) State the coefficient of x in 7x − 2. (c) Write the cost of 8 pencils at ₦p each.

lessons.title: Simplifying Expressions
lessons.content:
# Simplifying Expressions

We can simplify an expression by collecting like terms. Like terms have exactly the same letter part: 3a and 5a are like terms, but 3a and 5b are not. Add or subtract the coefficients and keep the letter.

Worked example 1: 3a + 5a = 8a. Worked example 2: 7x − 2x + 4 = 5x + 4. Worked example 3: 2a + 3b + a − b = (2a + a) + (3b − b) = 3a + 2b.

Removing brackets (expanding): multiply every term inside by the number outside. 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. 2(3y − 1) = 6y − 2. Worked example: 4(a + 2) + 3a = 4a + 8 + 3a = 7a + 8.

Practice: (a) 4m + 3m. (b) 6p − 2p + q. (c) 5(a + 2). (d) 2(x + 3) + 4x.

lessons.title: Substitution
lessons.content:
# Substitution

To substitute is to replace letters by given numbers and then work out the value. Always put the numbers in brackets at first, especially negatives, and follow the order of operations: brackets, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.

Worked example 1: If x = 4, then 3x − 5 = 3(4) − 5 = 12 − 5 = 7. Worked example 2: If a = 3 and b = −2, then 2a + b = 6 + (−2) = 4 and ab = 3 × (−2) = −6.

Worked example 3 (formula): The perimeter of a rectangle is P = 2(l + w). If l = 8 and w = 5, then P = 2(8 + 5) = 2 × 13 = 26.

Practice: (a) If x = 2, find 5x + 1. (b) If a = −1, find 4a. (c) Use A = lw to find the area when l = 7 and w = 3.

lessons.title: Simple Equations
lessons.content:
# Simple Equations

An equation says two expressions are equal. To solve it, find the value of the unknown that makes it true. The rule: whatever you do to one side you must do to the other side to keep the equation balanced.

Worked example 1: x + 7 = 15. Subtract 7 from both sides: x = 8. Worked example 2: 3x = 21. Divide both sides by 3: x = 7. Worked example 3: 2x − 5 = 9. Add 5 to both sides: 2x = 14. Divide by 2: x = 7. Worked example 4: 3x + 2 = x + 10. Subtract x from both sides: 2x + 2 = 10. Subtract 2: 2x = 8. So x = 4.

Always check: substitute your answer back. For example 4, left side 3(4) + 2 = 14 and right side 4 + 10 = 14. They match.

Practice: (a) x − 4 = 10. (b) 5x = 35. (c) 2x + 3 = 11. (d) x/4 = 6.

lessons.title: Forming Equations from Word Problems
lessons.content:
# Forming Equations from Word Problems

Many problems become easy when written as equations. Step 1: let a letter stand for the unknown. Step 2: translate the words into an equation. Step 3: solve it. Step 4: check the answer against the story.

Worked example 1: A number is multiplied by 3 and then 4 is added. The result is 19. Let the number be n. 3n + 4 = 19, 3n = 15, n = 5.

Worked example 2: Ade is 4 years older than Bola. The sum of their ages is 30. Let Bola be b. Then Ade is b + 4. b + b + 4 = 30, so 2b = 26 and b = 13. Bola is 13 and Ade is 17.

Worked example 3: A rectangle has a length that is 3 cm more than its width. Its perimeter is 26 cm. Let the width be w. Then 2(w + w + 3) = 26, so 2w + 3 = 13, 2w = 10 and w = 5. The width is 5 cm and the length is 8 cm.

Practice: (a) Doubling a number gives 18. Find it. (b) Two consecutive numbers add up to 25. Find them.

lessons.content:
# Indices

An index (or power) tells how many times a number is multiplied by itself. In 2³ the base is 2 and the index is 3, so 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. We read it as two to the power three.

The laws of indices: (1) a^m × a^n = a^(m+n). (2) a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n). (3) (a^m)^n = a^(mn). (4) a⁰ = 1.

Worked examples: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷ = 128. 5⁶ ÷ 5² = 5⁴ = 625. (3²)³ = 3⁶ = 729. 7⁰ = 1.

Notice that these laws only work when the bases are the same. 2³ × 3² cannot be combined this way; work it out as 8 × 9 = 72.

Practice: (a) 3² × 3³. (b) 10⁴ ÷ 10². (c) (2²)³. (d) 7⁰.

lessons.title: Number Patterns and Sequences
lessons.content:
# Number Patterns and Sequences

A sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule. In an arithmetic sequence the same number, the common difference, is added each time: 3, 7, 11, 15 has common difference 4, so the next term is 19. In a geometric sequence we multiply by the same number each time: 2, 6, 18, 54 has common ratio 3.

The nth term gives a formula for any position. For 3, 7, 11, 15 the common difference is 4, so the formula starts with 4n. For n = 1, 4n = 4 but the first term is 3, so subtract 1: nth term = 4n − 1. The 10th term is 4(10) − 1 = 39.

Special sequences: square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25; triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15; Fibonacci numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 where each term is the sum of the two before.

Practice: (a) Find the next term of 5, 9, 13. (b) The nth term is 3n + 2. Find the 5th term. (c) Continue 1, 2, 4, 8.

lessons.title: Simple Inequalities
lessons.content:
# Simple Inequalities

An inequality compares two values using symbols: < means less than, > means greater than, ≤ means less than or equal to, ≥ means greater than or equal to. The solution is usually a range of values rather than one number.

Solve inequalities as you solve equations. Worked example 1: x + 3 > 7 gives x > 4. Worked example 2: 2x ≤ 10 gives x ≤ 5. Worked example 3: x − 2 < 5 gives x < 7.

On a number line, an open circle shows that the end number is not included (< or >) and a filled circle shows it is included (≤ or ≥). The inequality 2 < x < 4 has only one whole-number solution, x = 3.

Practice: (a) Solve 3x > 12. (b) List the whole numbers that satisfy 1 ≤ x < 5.

lessons.title: Points, Lines and Angles
lessons.content:
# Points, Lines and Angles

A point marks a position and has no size. A line extends without end in both directions. A line segment has two end points and a fixed length. A ray starts at one point and goes on without end in one direction. Two lines that never meet, however far they are extended, are parallel; lines that cross at a right angle are perpendicular.

An angle is formed when two rays meet at a point called the vertex. We measure angles in degrees (°) with a protractor. Types: acute angle (less than 90°), right angle (exactly 90°), obtuse angle (between 90° and 180°), straight angle (exactly 180°) and reflex angle (between 180° and 360°). A full turn is 360°.

To use a protractor: place its centre on the vertex, line the zero line up with one arm, and read the scale where the other arm crosses, using the scale that starts at zero.

Practice: Classify each angle: 35°, 90°, 120°, 180°, 250°.

lessons.title: Angle Relationships
lessons.content:
# Angle Relationships

Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles at a point add up to 360°. Vertically opposite angles, formed when two straight lines cross, are equal. Two angles that add up to 90° are complementary; two that add up to 180° are supplementary.

Worked example 1: Two angles on a straight line are 3x and 2x. 3x + 2x = 180, so 5x = 180 and x = 36. The angles are 108° and 72°.

Worked example 2: The complement of 35° is 90° − 35° = 55°. The supplement of 110° is 180° − 110° = 70°.

Worked example 3: Angles at a point are 90°, 120°, 100° and x. 90 + 120 + 100 = 310, so x = 360 − 310 = 50°.

Practice: (a) Find the supplement of 110°. (b) Two straight lines cross and one angle is 65°. Find the vertically opposite angle.

lessons.title: Triangles
lessons.content:
# Triangles

A triangle has three sides and three angles. The angles always add up to 180°. By sides: an equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three 60° angles; an isosceles triangle has two equal sides and the two angles opposite them are equal; a scalene triangle has no equal sides. By angles: an acute triangle has all angles under 90°, a right-angled triangle has one angle of 90° and an obtuse triangle has one angle over 90°.

Worked example 1: Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°. The third is 180 − 110 = 70°.

Worked example 2: An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 40°. The two base angles are equal, so each is (180 − 40) ÷ 2 = 70°.

The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. If the interior angles are 50° and 60°, the exterior angle at the third vertex is 110°.

Practice: (a) A right-angled triangle has an angle of 35°. Find the third angle. (b) Find the angles of an equilateral triangle.

lessons.content:
# Quadrilaterals

A quadrilateral has four sides. Its angles add up to 360°. A square has four equal sides and four right angles. A rectangle has opposite sides equal and four right angles, and its diagonals are equal. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal and parallel. A rhombus has four equal sides with opposite angles equal. A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides. A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

Worked example: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 95° and 110°. 80 + 95 + 110 = 285, so the fourth angle is 360 − 285 = 75°.

Worked example 2: In a parallelogram, one angle is 70°. Opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles add up to 180°, so the angles are 70°, 110°, 70° and 110°.

Practice: (a) Find the fourth angle of a quadrilateral with 90°, 90° and 70°. (b) Which quadrilateral has equal diagonals and four right angles?

lessons.content:
# Perimeter and Area

Perimeter is the distance around a shape and is measured in units of length such as cm or m. Area is the amount of surface inside the shape and is measured in square units such as cm² or m². Formulae: rectangle P = 2(l + w), A = l × w; square A = s²; triangle A = ½ × b × h; parallelogram A = b × h.

Worked example 1: A rectangle is 12 cm by 7 cm. P = 2(12 + 7) = 38 cm. A = 12 × 7 = 84 cm².

Worked example 2: A triangle has base 10 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. A = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².

Worked example 3: A farmer wants to fence a rectangular plot 25 m by 16 m. The fence needs 2(25 + 16) = 82 m.

Practice: (a) Area of a square of side 9 m. (b) Area of a triangle with base 8 cm and height 5 cm. (c) Perimeter of a rectangle 15 cm by 4 cm.

lessons.content:
# The Circle

A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from a centre. The radius r is the distance from the centre to the edge; the diameter d passes through the centre and d = 2r. The circumference is the distance around the circle. The ratio of circumference to diameter is the same for every circle and is called π (pi), which is about 22/7 or 3.14.

Formulae: C = πd = 2πr and A = πr². Area is in square units.

Worked example (using π = 22/7): A circle has radius 7 cm. C = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm. A = 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 cm².

Worked example 2: A circular table has diameter 14 cm. C = 22/7 × 14 = 44 cm.

Practice: (a) Find the diameter of a circle with radius 3.5 cm. (b) Find the area of a circle of radius 7 cm using π = 22/7.

# Units of Measurement

Length: 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 cm = 10 mm. Mass: 1 kg = 1,000 g; 1 tonne = 1,000 kg. Capacity: 1 litre = 1,000 millilitres. Time: 1 hour = 60 minutes; 1 minute = 60 seconds; 1 day = 24 hours.

To change to a smaller unit, multiply; to change to a larger unit, divide. Worked example 1: 3.5 km = 3.5 × 1,000 = 3,500 m. Worked example 2: 2,400 g = 2,400 ÷ 1,000 = 2.4 kg. Worked example 3: 2 hours 45 minutes = (2 × 60) + 45 = 165 minutes.

Worked example 4: A bottle holds 750 mL. Four bottles hold 4 × 750 = 3,000 mL = 3 litres.

Practice: (a) Change 450 cm to m. (b) Change 3 L to mL. (c) Change 1.5 hours to minutes.

lessons.content:
# Collecting and Organising Data

Data are facts or numbers collected to answer a question. Methods of collection include observation, interviews, questionnaires and experiments. After collecting, organise the data with a tally and a frequency table. Frequency means how many times a value occurs.

Worked example: The marks of 10 pupils in a quiz are 5, 7, 6, 5, 8, 7, 5, 6, 7, 5. The frequency table is: mark 5 appears 4 times, mark 6 appears 2 times, mark 7 appears 3 times and mark 8 appears once. The frequencies add up to 4 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 10, the number of pupils.

The most common mark is 5. Always check that your frequencies add up to the total number of items.

Practice: Record the shoe sizes of ten classmates and make a tally and frequency table.

lessons.content:
# Charts, Mean, Median and Mode

A pictogram uses symbols to show data; a bar chart uses bars of equal width whose heights show frequencies. Label both axes and give the chart a title.

Averages: the mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are. The median is the middle value when the data are arranged in order (if there are two middle values, find their mean). The mode is the most frequent value. The range is the highest value minus the lowest.

Worked example 1: For 4, 6, 6, 7, 9 the mean is 32 ÷ 5 = 6.4, the median is 6, the mode is 6 and the range is 9 − 4 = 5.

Worked example 2: For 3, 5, 8, 10 the median is the mean of the two middle values: (5 + 8) ÷ 2 = 6.5.

Practice: (a) Mean of 2, 4, 6. (b) Mode of 3, 5, 5, 7, 9. (c) Median of 1, 3, 5, 7.

lessons.title: Living and Non-Living Things
lessons.content:
# Living and Non-Living Things

Living things are called organisms. All of them show seven characteristics, easily remembered as MRS GREN: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion and Nutrition. Movement means a change of position or parts. Respiration is the release of energy from food. Sensitivity is the ability to detect and respond to changes such as light, heat or touch. Growth is a permanent increase in size. Reproduction is the making of new organisms of the same kind. Excretion is the removal of waste made by the body. Nutrition is the taking in of food.

Non-living things such as stones, water and a motorcycle may move or change, but they do not show all seven characteristics. A car moves and uses fuel, yet it does not grow, reproduce or respond to its surroundings by itself.

Example: A yam tuber placed in a damp corner produces shoots. This shows growth and sensitivity to water. A stone in the same place does nothing.

Activity: Place a potted plant on a windowsill for five days and observe which way its leaves face. Which characteristic does this show?

lessons.title: The Cell
lessons.content:
# The Cell

The cell is the basic unit of life. Most cells are too small to see with the eye and must be viewed under a microscope. The word cell was first used by Robert Hooke in 1665 when he looked at thin slices of cork.

Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane (controls what enters and leaves), cytoplasm (a jelly where chemical reactions occur) and a nucleus (controls the cell's activities). Plant cells also have a cell wall made of cellulose that gives shape and support, chloroplasts that contain chlorophyll for making food, and a large central vacuole filled with cell sap. Animal cells have no cell wall or chloroplasts and have only small vacuoles.

Cells of the same kind form tissues; tissues form organs such as the heart; organs working together form a system such as the digestive system; and systems make up the organism.

Activity: Peel a thin layer from an onion, place it on a slide with a drop of water and view under a microscope. Draw the box-like cells you see and label the cell wall and nucleus.

lessons.title: Classification of Living Things
lessons.content:
# Classification of Living Things

Scientists sort organisms into groups so that they are easier to study. This is called classification. The two big groups are plants and animals. Animals are further divided into vertebrates, which have a backbone, and invertebrates, which do not.

The five classes of vertebrates are: fishes (live in water, have gills and scales, e.g. tilapia), amphibians (live on land and in water, e.g. frog), reptiles (dry scaly skin, e.g. lizard, snake, crocodile), birds (feathers, wings, lay eggs, e.g. hen) and mammals (hairy skin, give birth to live young and feed them with milk, e.g. goat, human, bat). Invertebrates include insects (six legs, e.g. ant), arachnids (eight legs, e.g. spider), crustaceans (e.g. crayfish) and molluscs (e.g. snail).

Plants are grouped into flowering plants, which bear seeds in fruits (mango, maize), and non-flowering plants such as ferns and mosses.

Example: A bat flies like a bird but has hair and feeds its young with milk, so it is a mammal.

lessons.title: Parts of a Flowering Plant
lessons.content:
# Parts of a Flowering Plant

A flowering plant has two main systems. The root system lies underground. Roots anchor the plant in the soil and absorb water and mineral salts. The shoot system lies above ground and has the stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds. The stem supports the plant and carries water and food between roots and leaves. The leaves make food by photosynthesis. The flower is the reproductive part, and after pollination and fertilisation it becomes the fruit, which holds the seeds.

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use sunlight to make food: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of light and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen. Plants take in carbon dioxide through tiny openings in leaves called stomata and release oxygen.

Plants may have a tap root system (one main root, as in mango and orange) or a fibrous root system (many thin roots of equal size, as in maize and grass).

Activity: Dig up a young maize plant and a pawpaw seedling carefully. Draw their roots and state which type each has.

lessons.title: Food and Nutrition
lessons.content:
# Food and Nutrition

Food provides energy, materials for growth and repair, and protection against disease. The seven classes of food are carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, vitamins, mineral salts, water and dietary fibre.

Carbohydrates give energy: yam, rice, cassava, bread. Proteins build and repair the body: beans, fish, meat, eggs, milk. Fats and oils give energy and form a store under the skin: palm oil, groundnut oil. Vitamins and mineral salts protect the body: vitamin C in oranges prevents scurvy; calcium in milk builds strong bones and teeth; iron in liver and green leafy vegetables forms blood. Water is needed for every body process. Fibre, found in vegetables and whole grains, helps food move through the gut.

A balanced diet contains all the food classes in the right amounts. Lack of a nutrient causes a deficiency disease: kwashiorkor (not enough protein), rickets (not enough vitamin D or calcium), scurvy (vitamin C), anaemia (iron) and goitre (iodine).

Activity: Write down everything you ate yesterday and sort it into the food classes. Which class was missing?

lessons.title: The Digestive System
lessons.content:
# The Digestive System

Digestion is the breaking down of food into small soluble particles that the blood can absorb. Food passes through the alimentary canal: the mouth, where teeth chew it and saliva begins to digest starch; the oesophagus, which carries it to the stomach by muscle squeezing (peristalsis); the stomach, where acid and enzymes digest protein; the small intestine, where digestion is completed and digested food is absorbed into the blood; the large intestine, where water is absorbed; and the rectum and anus, where undigested waste (faeces) is stored and removed.

The liver makes bile, which helps digest fats, and the pancreas makes digestive juices that flow into the small intestine.

Human teeth are of four types: incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding. Adults have 32 teeth. Care for them by brushing twice a day and visiting a dentist regularly.

Example: When you chew a piece of bread for a long time it begins to taste sweet, because saliva breaks starch into sugar.

lessons.title: Breathing and Respiration
lessons.content:
# Breathing and Respiration

Breathing (ventilation) is the movement of air into and out of the lungs. Air enters through the nose, passes down the trachea (windpipe), the bronchi and into tiny air sacs called alveoli. Oxygen passes from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the alveoli, a process called gas exchange. During inhalation the ribs move up and out and the diaphragm flattens, so the chest becomes bigger and air rushes in. During exhalation the opposite happens.

Respiration is different from breathing. It is the chemical process inside cells that releases energy from food: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy.

Inhaled air contains about 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Exhaled air contains about 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide, and more water vapour. You can show this by blowing through a straw into lime water, which turns milky because of carbon dioxide.

Smoking damages the alveoli and cilia of the lungs and is a major cause of lung disease.

lessons.title: Ecosystems and Food Chains
lessons.content:
# Ecosystems and Food Chains

An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings, such as a pond, a forest or a farm. Living components include producers, consumers and decomposers. Producers are green plants that make their own food. Consumers feed on other organisms: herbivores eat plants (primary consumers), carnivores eat animals (secondary or tertiary consumers) and omnivores eat both. Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

A food chain shows who eats whom. Example: grass → grasshopper → toad → snake → hawk. The arrows point in the direction of energy flow. Many interlinked food chains form a food web. The hawk is at the top of this chain.

Energy decreases along a food chain because each organism uses much of it for its own life, so food chains rarely have more than five links.

Activity: Draw a food chain for a pond in your area with at least four organisms.

lessons.title: Environmental Pollution and Conservation
lessons.content:
# Environmental Pollution and Conservation

Pollution is the addition of harmful substances to the environment. Air pollution comes from vehicle exhaust, burning refuse and industrial smoke. Water pollution comes from sewage, oil spills and dumping of waste in rivers. Land pollution comes from rubbish, plastic and chemicals. Noise pollution comes from generators, loud music and traffic.

Effects include respiratory illness, water-borne diseases such as cholera, death of fish and loss of farmland. Plastic and sachet water wrappers block drains and cause flooding when rains come.

Control measures: dispose of waste in bins, recycle and reuse plastics and bottles, treat sewage, plant trees (afforestation), use cleaner fuels and obey environmental sanitation rules. Conservation means using natural resources carefully so they last. Protecting forests, wildlife reserves such as Yankari Game Reserve, and saving water are examples.

Activity: Survey your school compound. List three sources of pollution and propose one solution for each.

lessons.title: Matter and Its States
lessons.content:
# Matter and Its States

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. It exists in three main states: solid, liquid and gas. A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume because its particles are packed closely and only vibrate in place. A liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container because its particles are close but can slide past each other. A gas has neither fixed shape nor fixed volume because its particles are far apart and move freely, so it fills any container.

Evidence of particles: a drop of ink spreads through water without stirring (diffusion), and the smell of cooking soup reaches you across a room. Gases can be squashed (compressed) because there is much space between particles; liquids and solids cannot be squashed easily.

Example: Water exists as ice (solid), water (liquid) and steam (gas), yet it is the same substance in all three states.

Activity: Put equal amounts of water in a bottle, a bowl and a cup. Observe how the volume and shape change.

lessons.title: Changes of State and Types of Change
lessons.content:
# Changes of State and Types of Change

When matter gains or loses heat it can change state. Melting changes a solid to a liquid (ice melts at 0°C). Freezing changes a liquid to a solid. Boiling or evaporation changes a liquid to a gas (water boils at 100°C at sea level). Condensation changes a gas to a liquid, as when water droplets form on a cold glass. Sublimation changes a solid straight to a gas without becoming liquid; camphor and ammonium chloride do this.

A physical change does not form a new substance and can usually be reversed: melting ice, dissolving sugar in water, tearing paper. A chemical change forms a new substance and is usually not easily reversed: burning wood, rusting of iron, cooking an egg, souring of milk. Signs of chemical change include a change in colour, a gas given off, light or heat produced, or a new smell.

Example: Iron nails left in damp air become brown. The brown rust is a new substance, so rusting is a chemical change.

Practice: Classify each as physical or chemical: boiling water, burning candle, melting wax, baking bread.

lessons.title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
lessons.content:
# Elements, Compounds and Mixtures

An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom and cannot be split into simpler substances by chemical means. About 118 elements are known. Each has a symbol: hydrogen H, oxygen O, carbon C, iron Fe, sodium Na, chlorine Cl, copper Cu, gold Au, silver Ag. Elements are grouped as metals (shiny, conduct heat and electricity, e.g. iron) and non-metals (dull, poor conductors, e.g. sulphur).

A compound is formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio. Water (H2O) is made of hydrogen and oxygen; table salt (NaCl) is sodium and chlorine; carbon dioxide (CO2) is carbon and oxygen. A compound has properties different from its elements.

A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined and can be separated by physical means. Examples: air, sea water, sand and water, a mixture of rice and beans. The parts keep their own properties.

Practice: Say whether each is an element, compound or mixture: oxygen, salt, soil, carbon dioxide, gold.

lessons.title: Separation of Mixtures
lessons.content:
# Separation of Mixtures

The method used depends on the properties of the substances. Sieving separates solids of different sizes, such as removing stones from beans. Decantation pours off a liquid from a settled solid. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper, as in sand and water. Evaporation removes water from a solution to leave the dissolved solid, as in getting salt from salt water in salt-making. Distillation separates a liquid from a solution by boiling it and condensing the vapour; it gives pure water from salt water. A magnet separates iron filings from sand. Chromatography separates coloured dyes in ink.

Worked example: To separate a mixture of sand, salt and iron filings. Step 1: use a magnet to remove the iron. Step 2: add water to dissolve the salt. Step 3: filter; sand stays on the filter paper. Step 4: evaporate the filtrate to obtain salt.

Practice: Name a method to separate (a) palm oil from water, (b) pure water from sea water, (c) stones from rice.

lessons.title: Air and Water
lessons.content:
# Air and Water

Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide, with varying water vapour. Oxygen supports burning and breathing. Nitrogen dilutes oxygen. Carbon dioxide is used by plants and turns lime water milky. A test for oxygen is that it relights a glowing splint. When a candle burns in a closed jar over water, the water rises by about one fifth because oxygen is used up.

Water is a colourless, tasteless, odourless liquid when pure. It freezes at 0°C, boils at 100°C and dissolves many substances, so it is called the universal solvent. Sources include rain, rivers, wells, boreholes and the sea.

Purification of water for drinking: sedimentation, filtration to remove solids, then chlorination or boiling to kill germs. Packaged water must carry the NAFDAC registration number. Dirty water can carry diseases such as cholera and typhoid.

Activity: Collect a muddy water sample and filter it through sand, gravel and cotton. Compare the filtered and unfiltered samples.

lessons.title: Forms and Sources of Energy
lessons.content:
# Forms and Sources of Energy

Energy is the ability to do work. Forms of energy include kinetic energy (energy of motion), potential energy (stored energy due to position, such as water behind a dam), heat, light, sound, chemical energy (in food, fuel and batteries), electrical energy and nuclear energy.

Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only change from one form to another. This is the law of conservation of energy. Examples: in a torch, chemical energy in the battery changes to electrical energy and then to light and heat. In a power station on the Niger such as Kainji, the potential energy of stored water becomes kinetic energy as it falls, then electrical energy through turbines.

Renewable sources will not run out: the sun (solar), wind, flowing water (hydro). Non-renewable sources are used faster than they form: crude oil, natural gas and coal. Nigeria produces large amounts of crude oil and gas, but solar power is growing for homes and businesses.

Activity: Trace the energy changes when you eat food, run, and feel warm.

lessons.title: Heat and Temperature
lessons.content:
# Heat and Temperature

Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hot object to a cold object. Temperature measures how hot or cold something is and is measured with a thermometer in degrees Celsius (°C). Heat is measured in joules. A lab thermometer uses mercury or alcohol in a narrow glass tube; a clinical thermometer measures body temperature, which is about 37°C in a healthy person.

Heat travels in three ways. Conduction is the flow of heat through a solid from particle to particle: a metal spoon in hot soup becomes hot. Metals are good conductors; wood, plastic and air are poor conductors, called insulators. Convection is the flow of heat in liquids and gases by the movement of the fluid itself: warm water rises and cool water sinks. Radiation is the transfer of heat by waves that need no material, as when the sun warms the Earth through space.

Applications: cooking pots are metal but handles are plastic or wood; houses have windows to let hot air out; light-coloured clothing reflects heat in the hot season.

Practice: Why does a cooking pot have a wooden handle?

lessons.title: Forces and Motion
lessons.content:
# Forces and Motion

A force is a push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N) with a spring balance. A force can start or stop motion, change speed or direction, or change the shape of an object. Common forces: gravity (pulls objects towards the Earth), friction (opposes motion between surfaces in contact), muscular force, magnetic force and upthrust (the upward push of a liquid).

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg), and does not change from place to place. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons. Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g). On Earth g is about 10 N/kg for JSS work.

Worked example: A bag of rice has a mass of 5 kg. Its weight is 5 × 10 = 50 N. On the Moon, where gravity is about one sixth as strong, its mass is still 5 kg but its weight is about 8 N.

Friction is useful in walking, braking and gripping, but it also causes wear and wastes energy as heat. We reduce it using oil, grease and smooth surfaces and increase it with rough soles and treaded tyres.

Practice: Find the weight of a 12 kg bag on Earth.

lessons.title: Simple Machines
lessons.content:
# Simple Machines

A machine is a device that makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force. Simple machines include the lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, wedge and screw. A lever turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum: a see-saw, a wheelbarrow, scissors and a crowbar are levers. A pulley changes the direction of a force, as when raising a bucket from a well. An inclined plane (ramp) lets us raise a load with less force over a longer distance. A wheel and axle is used in a bicycle and a steering wheel.

Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort. Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of force, measured in joules (J).

Worked example 1: A crowbar lifts a load of 600 N using an effort of 200 N. The mechanical advantage is 600 ÷ 200 = 3.

Worked example 2: A man pushes a barrow with a force of 50 N for 4 m. Work done = 50 × 4 = 200 J.

Practice: A pulley system lifts a 900 N load with a 300 N effort. Find the mechanical advantage.

lessons.title: Meaning and Importance of Technology
lessons.content:
# Meaning and Importance of Technology

Technology is the use of scientific knowledge, tools and skills to solve practical problems and meet human needs. Science explains how things work; technology applies that knowledge to make useful things. Technology is as old as humankind. Early people made stone tools, fire, pottery and farming tools. Nigeria has a long technology tradition: iron smelting at Nok, bronze casting at Igbo-Ukwu and Benin, cloth weaving and dyeing, and calabash and pottery making.

Modern technology touches everyday life: mobile phones for communication, tractors for farming, solar panels for power, machines for processing food and vehicles for transport. It brings benefits such as faster communication, higher food production, better healthcare and more jobs. It also brings problems such as pollution, loss of some manual jobs and misuse of devices.

Example: A hand-held grinding stone and a modern grinding machine both process grain. The machine is faster because of improved technology.

Activity: List five technological devices in your home and state the problem each solves.

lessons.title: Tools and Workshop Safety
lessons.content:
# Tools and Workshop Safety

Tools make work easier and more accurate. Measuring tools: metre rule, tape, try square and vernier calliper. Cutting tools: hand saw, hacksaw (for metal), chisel and plane. Striking tools: hammers and mallets. Holding tools: vice, pliers and clamps. Turning tools: screwdriver and spanner. Always use the right tool for the job, keep it sharp, clean and stored properly.

Safety rules in a workshop: wear overalls, safety goggles and gloves; tie up long hair; wear closed shoes; keep the floor clear and dry; never run; report accidents at once; know where the fire extinguisher and first aid box are; do not use a damaged tool and switch off machines before leaving them.

Example: A hammer with a loose head is dangerous because the head may fly off. It should be repaired before use.

Activity: Make a safety poster for your school workshop with five rules.

lessons.content:
# Communication Technology

Communication is the passing of information from one person or place to another. Traditional methods included talking drums, town criers, gongs, smoke signals and messengers. Modern methods include the postal service, telephone, radio, television, newspapers and the internet. Mobile (GSM) services began in Nigeria in 2001 and led to rapid growth in phones, banking apps and online learning.

A communication system has a sender, a message, a channel and a receiver; feedback tells the sender the message has been understood. Radio and television use radio waves, while phones use cables or radio signals.

Safe use: never share passwords, do not believe every message online, respect others when posting, and avoid meeting strangers you met online. Remember that communication devices should not distract you from studies.

Activity: Compare how news of a school event was spread in your grandparents' time and today.

lessons.title: Materials and Their Properties
lessons.content:
# Materials and Their Properties

Materials are the substances used for making things. Natural materials come from nature: wood, cotton, clay, rubber, stone, wool. Man-made materials are manufactured: plastics, nylon, glass, cement, steel. Wood may be hardwood (iroko, mahogany, teak) from broad-leaved trees or softwood (pine) from conifers. Metals are strong, shiny, malleable (can be hammered into shape), ductile (can be drawn into wires) and good conductors: iron, steel, aluminium and copper. Plastics are light, waterproof and cheap, but many do not rot and cause waste.

Important properties: strength, hardness, elasticity (returns to shape after stretching), conductivity, density and resistance to rust or rot. We choose a material for its properties: copper for electric wires because it conducts well; plastic for cable covering because it insulates; rubber for tyres because it is elastic and tough.

Example: Aluminium is used for cooking pots because it conducts heat, is light and does not rust easily.

Activity: Collect six materials and test whether each bends, floats, conducts electricity or dissolves.

lessons.title: Introduction to Electricity
lessons.content:
# Introduction to Electricity

Electricity is a form of energy produced by the movement of electric charges. A simple electric circuit has a source (cell or battery), conducting wires, a load (bulb) and usually a switch. The bulb lights only when the circuit is a complete closed loop. An open circuit has a gap and no current flows.

Current is measured in amperes (A) and voltage in volts (V). Conductors let current flow easily: copper, aluminium, iron and graphite. Insulators do not: rubber, plastic, dry wood and glass. In a series circuit there is one path and if one bulb fails all go out. In a parallel circuit there are branches, so one bulb failing does not affect the others, which is how house wiring is arranged.

Safety: never touch bare wires or switches with wet hands; never put metal objects into sockets; do not overload sockets; keep away from fallen power lines; use fuses and earthing; and call a qualified electrician for repairs.

Activity: Build a simple circuit with a cell, bulb, wires and switch and draw the circuit using standard symbols.

lessons.title: Magnetism
lessons.content:
# Magnetism

A magnet attracts magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Materials like wood, plastic and copper are non-magnetic. Every magnet has two poles, north and south, where the force is strongest. Unlike poles attract and like poles repel. If you break a magnet, each piece becomes a new magnet with two poles.

The Earth behaves like a giant magnet. A freely-hanging magnet or compass needle points towards magnetic north. Compasses are used by sailors, pilots and hikers.

Magnets can be made by stroking a steel bar with one pole of a magnet in one direction, or by passing current through a coil of wire. Uses of magnets: compasses, fridge doors, loudspeakers, door catches, electric motors and separation of iron from scrap.

Keep magnets away from phones, cards and computer disks because they can damage stored data.

Activity: Test ten objects with a magnet and record which are magnetic.

lessons.title: Personal Hygiene and First Aid
lessons.content:
# Personal Hygiene and First Aid

Personal hygiene means the practices that keep the body clean and healthy. Bathe daily, brush your teeth twice a day, wash your hands with soap and water after using the toilet and before eating, keep your nails short, wear clean clothes and keep hair clean. Clean surroundings, clean water and safe food storage also protect health.

First aid is the immediate help given to an injured or ill person before a doctor arrives. Aims: preserve life, prevent the condition from worsening and promote recovery. For a minor cut: wash your hands, rinse the wound with clean water, press with a clean cloth to stop bleeding, then cover it with a clean dressing. For a burn: cool it under cool running water for about 10 to 20 minutes and cover loosely with a clean non-fluffy cloth; do not apply butter, toothpaste or oil. For a nosebleed: sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes. For a fainting person: lay them down and raise their legs. Serious injuries need a health worker at once.

A first aid box should contain plasters, bandages, gauze, antiseptic, scissors and gloves.

Activity: Role-play treating a minor cut with a partner.

lessons.title: Common Diseases and Prevention
lessons.content:
# Common Diseases and Prevention

A communicable disease can spread from one person to another. Malaria is caused by a parasite called Plasmodium and is spread by the female Anopheles mosquito. Prevent it by sleeping under insecticide-treated nets, clearing stagnant water where mosquitoes breed and keeping bushes short. Cholera is caused by a bacterium and spread by contaminated water and food. Typhoid is also spread by contaminated food and water. Prevention: drink safe water, wash hands, cook food well and use clean toilets.

Vaccines train the body to fight specific diseases. Children in Nigeria are vaccinated against polio, measles, tuberculosis and others at health centres. Common signs that need a health worker's advice include fever, vomiting and diarrhoea, especially in children. Self-medication is dangerous; see a trained health worker.

Non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and high blood pressure do not spread from person to person and are linked to diet, lifestyle and heredity.

Activity: Make a poster on how to prevent malaria in your home.

lessons.title: Drug Use and Abuse
lessons.content:
# Drug Use and Abuse

A drug is any substance that changes how the body or mind works. Medicines are drugs used to prevent or cure disease and must be taken only as prescribed or directed by a trained health worker. Drug misuse is taking a medicine wrongly. Drug abuse is using a substance for non-medical reasons or in harmful ways. Commonly abused substances include alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, some cough syrups and certain pain killers.

Effects of abuse: damage to the brain, liver, lungs and heart; poor performance in school; accidents; mental illness; family problems; crime and addiction, where the person cannot stop using the substance. The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) enforces Nigerian drug laws and runs programmes against abuse.

Staying safe: learn the facts, make friends who respect your choice, say no firmly, avoid places where drugs are used, and talk to a parent, teacher or counsellor if pressured. People with addiction can recover with help from health workers and counsellors.

Activity: Role-play politely refusing a friend who offers you something harmful.

lessons.title: Technology and Technological Development
lessons.content:
# Technology and Technological Development

Technology is the practical use of knowledge, tools and materials to produce goods and services that meet human needs. Basic Technology introduces the main areas of this work: woodwork, metalwork, building construction, technical drawing, electrical work, plumbing and the mechanics of machines.

Technology has developed in stages. Early people used stone, bone and wood tools. Later came the use of fire, pottery, metal smelting, the wheel, and farming tools. The steam engine began the industrial age, followed by electricity, the internal combustion engine, computers and mobile communication. Each stage made production faster and goods cheaper.

Traditional technologies in Nigeria include blacksmithing, weaving, dyeing (as in Kano and Abeokuta), wood carving, pottery and leatherwork. Many of these still support families and communities and now work alongside modern machines.

Example: A farmer using a cutlass and hoe can clear a small farm slowly. A tractor clears the same land in a fraction of the time. Both are technology; the tractor is more advanced.

Activity: Make a timeline of five technologies that changed how people travel.

lessons.title: Workshop Hazards, Safety and Fire
lessons.content:
# Workshop Hazards, Safety and Fire

A hazard is anything that can cause harm. Workshop hazards include sharp tools, flying chips, moving machines, electric shock, noise, dust, fumes, slippery floors and fire. Safety rules prevent accidents: wear protective equipment such as goggles, gloves, apron and boots; keep the floor clean; return tools after use; never fool around with machines; report all accidents to the teacher; and know the position of the exits and fire extinguishers.

Fire needs three things, the fire triangle: heat, fuel and oxygen. Removing any one puts the fire out. Water cools a fire and is suitable for wood and paper but must never be used on electrical or oil fires. A carbon dioxide extinguisher can be used on electrical and flammable liquid fires. Foam and dry powder extinguishers are also used. A bucket of dry sand smothers small oil fires. Modern extinguishers have a red body and a coloured label that shows the type.

If a fire starts: raise the alarm, switch off the power if it is safe, and leave the building through the nearest exit. Fight only small fires and never put yourself at risk.

Activity: Draw the layout of your school workshop and mark the fire extinguisher, first aid box and exits.

lessons.title: Measuring and Marking Out Tools
lessons.content:
# Measuring and Marking Out Tools

Accurate work starts with accurate measuring and marking out. Common tools: the steel rule (graduated in millimetres and centimetres), the measuring tape (flexible, for long lengths), the try square (checks and marks angles of 90°), the marking gauge (scratches a line parallel to an edge of wood), the scriber (marks lines on metal), the dividers (mark circles and step off equal distances) and the spirit level (checks horizontal and vertical).

Marking out on wood is done with a sharp pencil or a marking knife; on metal a scriber is used. A centre punch makes a small dent so that a drill does not wander. The rule is: measure twice, cut once. When cutting, saw on the waste side of the line so that the finished piece keeps its correct size.

Worked example 1: A board 1,200 mm long is to be cut into 5 equal pieces. Each piece is 1,200 ÷ 5 = 240 mm (ignoring the width of the saw cut).

Worked example 2: A plank is 2.4 m (2,400 mm) long. How many 350 mm pieces can be cut from it? 2,400 ÷ 350 = 6 remainder 300, so 6 pieces and a 300 mm offcut.

Practice: A 3 m pole is cut into pieces of 450 mm. How many pieces, and what is left over?

lessons.title: Woodwork Tools and Joints
lessons.content:
# Woodwork Tools and Joints

Cutting tools for wood: the cross-cut saw (cuts across the grain), the rip saw (along the grain) and the tenon saw (fine, for joints). The jack plane smooths and reduces the thickness of timber. Chisels cut grooves and joints and are struck with a mallet. A brace and bit or hand drill makes holes. Hammers drive nails; a claw hammer also pulls them out. G-clamps and the bench hook hold work.

A joint connects two pieces of wood. The butt joint places two ends together and is held with nails or glue (the simplest, weakest). A halving or lap joint removes half the thickness of both pieces so they fit flush. The mortise and tenon joint, with a projecting tenon fitting into a slot, is strong and used for doors and tables. The dowel joint uses wooden pegs. The mitre joint is cut at 45° to make corners on picture frames. The dovetail joint is very strong and used for drawers.

Always cut with the grain where possible, keep chisels sharp and cut away from your body.

Activity: Make a simple halving joint from two offcuts and test its strength.

lessons.title: Metalwork Tools and Basic Operations
lessons.content:
# Metalwork Tools and Basic Operations

Hand tools for metal: the hacksaw (cuts metal, with the blade's teeth pointing forward), files (flat, round, half-round and triangular, for smoothing and shaping), the centre punch (marks a drilling point), the ball-pein hammer (for shaping and punching), snips (cut sheet metal), pliers, the bench vice (holds work firmly) and the steel rule and scriber for marking out.

Basic operations: marking out, cutting, filing, drilling, bending and joining. Joining methods include riveting, bolting, soldering (with a low-melting alloy, used for electronics and tin ware), brazing and welding (where metals are melted and fused together, using electric arc or gas). Always grip work tightly in the vice, never use a file without a handle and wear goggles when chipping or grinding.

Example: To drill a hole in a steel plate, first mark the centre with a scriber, then make a dent with the centre punch, clamp the plate and drill slowly with a little oil.

Activity: File the edge of a mild steel strip until it is smooth and straight.

lessons.title: Wood: Types, Seasoning and Preservation
lessons.content:
# Wood: Types, Seasoning and Preservation

Timber comes from trees. Hardwoods come from broad-leaved trees, are usually dense and durable and include iroko, mahogany, teak and opepe. Softwoods come from conifers such as pine and are lighter and easier to work. These words describe the type of tree, not always the hardness: balsa is a very soft hardwood.

Freshly cut timber contains a lot of moisture and will warp, shrink and crack if used. Seasoning removes the moisture. Natural (air) seasoning stacks timber under shade with spaces between layers so air flows; it takes months. Kiln seasoning dries timber in a heated chamber in days. Defects include knots, shakes (cracks), warping, twisting, rot and insect attack.

Preservation protects wood from decay, termites and weather using paint, varnish, creosote or chemical treatment. Manufactured boards make better use of timber: plywood (thin layers glued with grains crossing), blockboard, chipboard and fibre board.

Activity: Collect small samples of three local woods and describe their colour, weight and grain.

lessons.title: Metals and Alloys
lessons.content:
# Metals and Alloys

Metals are grouped as ferrous (containing iron) and non-ferrous (not containing iron). Ferrous metals include cast iron (hard but brittle, used for engine blocks), wrought iron (tough, used for gates) and steel (iron with a little carbon). Mild steel contains little carbon and is easy to bend and weld; high carbon steel is very hard and used for tools. Non-ferrous metals include copper (good conductor, used for wires and pipes), aluminium (light, resists corrosion, used for pots and roofing sheets), zinc, lead and tin.

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements to improve its properties. Brass is copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin; steel is iron and carbon; solder is an alloy used for joining.

Properties: malleable (can be hammered flat), ductile (can be drawn into wire), tough, hard, brittle (breaks without bending) and elastic. Iron rusts when exposed to oxygen and water. Protect against rust by painting, oiling or galvanising, which coats iron with zinc.

Activity: List six metal objects in your home and say whether each is ferrous or non-ferrous.

lessons.title: Plastics, Rubber, Glass and Ceramics
lessons.content:
# Plastics, Rubber, Glass and Ceramics

Plastics are made from chemicals mostly obtained from crude oil. Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be reshaped; examples are polythene (bags, bowls), PVC (pipes) and nylon. Thermosetting plastics set hard when moulded and cannot be softened again; examples are Bakelite (plugs, switches) and melamine (plates). Plastics are light, waterproof, do not rust and are cheap, but they do not rot easily and cause waste.

Natural rubber comes from latex tapped from rubber trees grown in parts of Edo, Delta, Ondo and other states. It is elastic and used for tyres, boots and seals. Synthetic rubbers are made from chemicals.

Glass is made by melting sand with soda ash and limestone. It is transparent, hard and brittle. Ceramics are made from clay shaped and fired in a kiln: bricks, tiles, pots, sanitary ware and insulators.

Activity: Sort ten household items into plastic, rubber, glass or ceramic.

lessons.title: Building Materials: Cement, Sand, Concrete and Blocks
lessons.content:
# Building Materials: Cement, Sand, Concrete and Blocks

Cement is a grey powder made by burning limestone and clay. Mixed with water it sets hard. Sand is fine aggregate and gravel or crushed granite is coarse aggregate. Mortar is cement and sand mixed with water and used for bonding blocks and plastering. Concrete is cement, sand and coarse aggregate with water.

Mix proportions are given by volume. A common mix for general concrete is 1 : 2 : 4 (one part cement, two parts sand and four parts gravel). Mortar for blockwork is often 1 : 6 (cement to sand). Worked example: If 3 head pans of cement are used for a 1 : 2 : 4 mix, then sand is 3 × 2 = 6 head pans and gravel is 3 × 4 = 12 head pans.

Use only enough water to make the mix workable; too much weakens it. Concrete gains strength by curing, which means keeping it damp for about seven days.

Sandcrete blocks are moulded from cement, sand and water. Common sizes in Nigeria are 450 × 225 × 225 mm (9 inch) and 450 × 225 × 150 mm (6 inch). Blocks must be cured and not used until properly hardened.

Practice: For a 1 : 2 : 4 mix with 5 pans of cement, find the amounts of sand and gravel.
