lessons.title: Drawing Instruments and Materials
lessons.content:
# Drawing Instruments and Materials

Technical drawing is the language of technologists. It gives exact information about the shape and size of an object. Instruments needed: drawing board, T-square, set squares (45° and 30°/60°), a pair of compasses, dividers, protractor, rule, pencils, eraser, drawing paper, masking tape or clips, and sharpener.

Pencil grades: H pencils are hard and make light thin lines (2H for construction lines); HB is medium and is used for lettering and general lines; B pencils are soft and make dark thick lines. A sharp pencil is essential for accuracy.

Fix the paper to the board with tape so that its lower edge is parallel to the T-square blade. Always keep the head of the T-square pressed against the left edge of the board (for right-handed users) when drawing horizontal lines. Draw vertical lines by sliding a set square along the T-square and drawing upward.

With the two set squares used together angles of 15°, 75°, 105° and 120° can also be drawn.

Activity: Fix a sheet of paper, draw a border 10 mm from the edges and a title block at the bottom right.

lessons.title: Types of Lines and Lettering
lessons.content:
# Types of Lines and Lettering

Different lines have different meanings. A continuous thick line shows the visible outline of an object. A continuous thin line is used for construction lines, dimension lines and projection lines. A dashed line shows hidden edges. A chain line (alternate long and short dashes) shows centre lines. Keep line thickness and darkness consistent.

Lettering must be clear and neat. Technical lettering is usually in single-stroke capital letters of equal height, between about 3 and 5 mm. Draw two light guide lines to keep letters at the same height, and leave equal spacing between letters and words.

Example: A circle's centre is marked with crossing chain lines. A hole behind a surface that cannot be seen from the front is drawn with dashed lines.

Activity: Letter your name and your school using 5 mm capitals between guide lines.

lessons.title: Dimensioning and the Title Block
lessons.content:
# Dimensioning and the Title Block

Dimensions tell the size of an object. A dimension line is a thin line with arrowheads at each end showing the distance measured. Extension lines extend from the edges of the object and are thin lines that touch the object slightly but extend a little beyond the dimension line. The figure is written above the dimension line, usually in millimetres, and read from the bottom or the right of the sheet. Do not repeat the same dimension and do not use outlines as dimension lines.

The title block is a small box, usually at the lower right of the sheet, giving the title of the drawing, name of the draughtsman, date, scale, projection symbol, and the school or company. It makes sure the drawing can be identified and understood.

Worked example: A rectangular board is 600 mm long and 300 mm wide. Draw it, and place the dimension 600 below the drawing and 300 to the right with arrowheads and extension lines.

Practice: Dimension a rectangle of 120 mm by 80 mm.

lessons.title: Geometrical Construction: Lines and Angles
lessons.content:
# Geometrical Construction: Lines and Angles

To bisect a line AB: with the compass opened to more than half of AB, draw arcs above and below the line from A, then with the same radius draw arcs from B so they cross. Join the two crossing points. This line cuts AB into two equal parts at right angles, so it is also the perpendicular bisector.

To draw an angle of 60°: draw a base line, put the compass point on the left end, draw a long arc across the line; without changing the radius, put the compass point on the arc and mark a second arc across the first. Join the left end to the crossing point. The angle is 60° because it is part of an equilateral triangle. Bisecting 60° gives 30°, and adding 60° and 30° gives 90°.

To bisect an angle: draw an arc crossing both arms, then from these two points draw equal arcs so they intersect; join the vertex to the intersection.

To construct a perpendicular at a point on a line: mark equal distances on either side of the point, then draw arcs above the line from each mark with a larger radius and join their crossing to the point.

Practice: Draw a 70 mm line and bisect it. Construct an angle of 45° by bisecting 90°.

lessons.content:
# Geometrical Construction: Triangles, Circles and Polygons

To construct a triangle with three given sides, for example 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm: draw the longest side as the base, then from one end draw an arc with a radius of one of the other sides, and from the other end draw an arc with the third side. Join the crossing to both ends. An equilateral triangle needs three equal sides: use the compass at the same radius from both ends.

A regular hexagon has six equal sides, and each side is equal to the radius of its circumscribing circle. Draw a circle, then keep the compass at the same radius, step round the circumference from any point and mark six points. Join them in order.

To draw a square of given side, draw the base, erect perpendiculars at each end of the same length and join the tops. To inscribe a circle in a triangle, bisect any two angles; the intersection is the centre of the circle and the distance to a side is the radius.

Check your construction by measuring: sides and angles should match the figures given.

Practice: Draw a hexagon of side 30 mm and a triangle of sides 4, 5 and 6 cm.

lessons.title: Scale Drawing
lessons.content:
# Scale Drawing

Objects too large to draw full size are drawn smaller using a scale. Objects too small are enlarged. The scale 1 : 5 means that 1 unit on the drawing represents 5 of the same units on the real object. Scale 1 : 1 is full size, and 2 : 1 is an enlargement to twice the size. Always write the scale on the drawing.

Worked example 1: A wall is 2.4 m long. Draw it at a scale of 1 : 20. 2.4 m = 2,400 mm. 2,400 ÷ 20 = 120 mm on paper.

Worked example 2: A room measures 4 m by 3 m. Draw it at 1 : 50. 4,000 ÷ 50 = 80 mm and 3,000 ÷ 50 = 60 mm. So draw a rectangle 80 mm by 60 mm.

Worked example 3: A line measures 45 mm on a drawing of scale 1 : 100. The real length is 45 × 100 = 4,500 mm = 4.5 m.

A scale rule can be used to read distances directly. Dimensions on the drawing are always the real sizes, not the sizes drawn.

Practice: Draw a classroom 8 m by 6 m at a scale of 1 : 100.

lessons.title: Isometric and Oblique Drawing
lessons.content:
# Isometric and Oblique Drawing

Pictorial drawings show an object in three dimensions the way you see it. In isometric drawing, the vertical edges are drawn vertical and the two other sets of edges are drawn at 30° to the horizontal. All lengths along these three axes are drawn to the same scale. A cube drawn isometrically shows three faces, and each face looks like a rhombus.

Steps: draw a light vertical line and two light lines at 30° from its base to form the axes; mark the length, width and height along them; draw the parallel edges; and darken the outline. A circle in isometric becomes an ellipse.

In oblique drawing, the front face is drawn in its true shape and the receding edges are drawn at 45° to the horizontal. In cabinet oblique the receding lengths are halved, so a 60 mm deep block would be drawn with 30 mm receding lines.

Activity: Draw a cuboid 60 × 40 × 30 mm in isometric.

Remember that isometric drawings are not true projections; they are useful for explanations and instructions.

lessons.title: Orthographic Projection
lessons.content:
# Orthographic Projection

Orthographic projection shows an object in separate views drawn at right angles to each other so that its true shapes and sizes appear. In first-angle projection, widely used in Nigerian schools, the object is placed in front of a vertical plane (V.P.) and above a horizontal plane (H.P.). The views are the front elevation (view from the front), plan (view from above) and end elevation (view from the side).

In first-angle projection the plan is drawn below the front elevation, and the end elevation seen from the left is drawn on the right of the front elevation. Corresponding points must line up using thin projection lines. Hidden parts are drawn with dashed lines.

Example: A rectangular block 60 mm long, 40 mm wide and 30 mm high. Front elevation: rectangle 60 × 30. Plan: rectangle 60 × 40 drawn below it. End elevation: rectangle 40 × 30 drawn to the right.

Practice: Draw the three views of a block 50 × 30 × 20 mm with a 10 mm square hole through its height.

lessons.title: Freehand Sketching and Care of Instruments
lessons.content:
# Freehand Sketching and Care of Instruments

A freehand sketch is a drawing made without instruments, using only a pencil and paper. It is used to record ideas quickly and to explain things to others. Good sketches have correct proportions, clear outlines and neat lines. Practise by drawing straight lines in light movements of the whole arm and by using light guidelines for shapes. Start by drawing a rectangle or box that holds the object, then add details.

Sketch a simple object such as a stool: draw its overall box, divide it into the top, legs and rails, add thickness, then darken the lines. Add labels and approximate dimensions.

Care of instruments: keep set squares and T-squares clean and free from scratches; do not use them to cut paper; keep the compass point sharp and tightened; store pencils sharpened; clean hands before drawing; wipe your board; and keep all tools in a case. Always check that the drawing room is tidy before leaving.

Activity: Sketch your school bag from two views and label its parts.

lessons.title: Parts of a Building
lessons.content:
# Parts of a Building

A building is a structure with walls and a roof that shelters people and property. The main parts are, from the ground upward: the foundation, which carries the weight of the whole building to the soil; the damp-proof course (DPC), a layer of waterproof material laid in the wall at least 150 mm above ground level to stop moisture rising; the walls; the floor; doors and windows, with a lintel (a beam) above each opening to carry the wall above; the roof; and the ceiling.

Buildings may be residential (houses, flats), commercial (shops, offices), industrial (factories, workshops) or public (schools, hospitals, mosques and churches).

Before building, the owner needs a plan approved by the town planning authority, a site that is cleared, and sound materials. A building plan shows layout, sizes and positions of rooms.

Activity: Sketch the front view of a simple bungalow and label foundation, DPC, wall, lintel, window, door and roof.

lessons.title: Building Tools and Site Safety
lessons.content:
# Building Tools and Site Safety

Building tools: the trowel (spreads mortar), hand float (smooths plaster), spirit level (checks horizontal and vertical), plumb bob (checks vertical), line and pins (keep courses straight), measuring tape, spade and shovel (for mixing and moving sand and cement), head pan, wheelbarrow, mason's hammer, and mould for blocks.

Mixing: measure materials in the correct proportions, mix dry cement and sand first until evenly coloured, then add water slowly. Do not mix more than can be used within about an hour because the cement begins to set.

Site safety: wear boots, hard hats and gloves; keep the site tidy; fence off open trenches; use sound scaffolding and ladders and never overload them; cover the mouth and nose when handling cement because dust harms the lungs; lift with a straight back; keep children away from the site.

Activity: List the tools you would need to lay one course of blocks and say what each does.

lessons.title: Foundations and Walls
lessons.content:
# Foundations and Walls

The foundation spreads the load of the building over enough soil so that it does not sink or crack. Types: the strip foundation is a continuous strip of concrete under the walls and is common for houses; the pad foundation supports single columns; the raft foundation is a thick slab covering the whole area and is used on weak soil. The depth and type depend on the soil, load and nearby water. For large or tall buildings an engineer must decide.

Walls are built in horizontal layers called courses. Bonding means arranging blocks or bricks so that vertical joints in one course do not lie directly above those in the course below, which spreads loads and strengthens the wall. A stretcher is the long face of a block; a header is the end face. In stretcher bond all blocks are laid with their long faces showing, with each course overlapping the one below by half a block.

Use a line and spirit level to keep each course level, keep joints about 10 mm thick and fill them fully with mortar.

Activity: Draw three courses of blocks in stretcher bond.

lessons.title: Concrete Work and Block Making
lessons.content:
# Concrete Work and Block Making

Concrete is used for foundations, floors, columns, beams and slabs. The quality depends on the proportion of materials, the quality of aggregates and water, and curing. Use clean sand and gravel, and clean water without salt or oil. Steel bars (reinforcement) are placed in concrete for beams and slabs because concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension; this is called reinforced concrete.

Formwork is the temporary mould that holds fresh concrete in shape until it hardens; it is removed only when the concrete is strong enough, usually after several days. Compaction removes air pockets by tamping or vibrating.

Making sandcrete blocks: mix cement and sand at about 1 : 6 by volume with just enough water to give a damp mix that holds together when squeezed, fill the block mould, compact, remove the mould and place the block on a flat surface in the shade. Sprinkle water on the blocks for at least seven days.

Worked example: A block-making machine uses a 1 : 6 mix. If 2 bags of cement are used, the sand is 6 times as much by volume, that is 12 bag-volumes.

Practice: What amount of sand is needed for 4 pans of cement in a 1 : 6 mix?

lessons.title: Roofs and Roofing Materials
lessons.content:
# Roofs and Roofing Materials

The roof covers the building, keeps out rain and sun and carries its own weight. Types of roof: flat (almost level, with a slight fall for drainage), lean-to or mono-pitch (one slope), gable (two slopes meeting at a ridge) and hip (slopes on all four sides). Tropical areas with heavy rain need steeper roofs for fast drainage.

A timber roof consists of a wall plate (on top of the wall), rafters (sloping members), a ridge board, purlins (horizontal supports) and roof trusses (triangular frames carrying the covering). Coverings include aluminium and zinc sheets, clay or concrete tiles, and thatch in some rural areas. Roof sheets should be fixed with the right nails or screws and sealed to avoid leaks. The edges overhang the walls to throw rain away from them.

Guttering and downpipes carry rain water away from the roof, protecting the walls and foundation from erosion.

Activity: Draw a gable roof, label the ridge, rafter and purlin and describe how rain water leaves the roof.

lessons.title: Electrical Installation Basics
lessons.content:
# Electrical Installation Basics

Electricity supplied to Nigerian homes is alternating current at 230 V and 50 Hz. A wiring system needs cables (copper conductors covered by insulation), switches, sockets, light fittings, a distribution board with fuses or circuit breakers, and an earth connection. In modern cables the colours are brown for live, blue for neutral and green with yellow stripes for earth. Typically, 1.5 mm² cable is used for lighting circuits and 2.5 mm² for socket circuits.

A fuse contains a thin wire that melts when too much current flows, breaking the circuit; a circuit breaker does the same job but can be reset. The earth wire carries a fault current safely to the ground so that people are not shocked. Never replace a fuse with a wire or a higher rating.

Safety: switch off at the main before working; only qualified electricians should do house wiring; do not touch wet appliances or sockets; keep cables away from heat and water; and never overload a socket with many appliances.

Activity: Identify the live, neutral and earth connections on a three-pin plug.

lessons.title: Basic Plumbing
lessons.content:
# Basic Plumbing

Plumbing is the installation and repair of pipes that carry water into buildings and waste out. Pipe materials: PVC (light, rust-free, used for cold water and drains), galvanised iron (strong, rusts after long use), copper and PPR. Fittings: elbow (changes direction), tee (makes a branch), coupling or socket (joins two pipes), union (allows disconnection), reducer (joins different sizes), gate valve and taps.

Tools: pipe wrench, hacksaw, pipe cutter, die stock for threading, spanner, and measuring tape. PVC pipes are joined with solvent cement; threaded pipe joints are sealed with PTFE (plumber's) tape.

A trap is a bend that holds water to block foul gas from the drain from entering the room. Water in houses is often stored in tanks above the roof so gravity can push water through the pipes. A dripping tap wastes much water; a worn washer is the common cause and can be replaced.

Safety: switch off the water supply before repair, keep joints tight and clean, and wash hands after handling waste pipes.

Activity: Draw a layout of a simple bathroom supply and drainage system.

lessons.title: Engines and Everyday Machines
lessons.content:
# Engines and Everyday Machines

An engine converts the chemical energy in fuel to mechanical energy. Most vehicles and small generators use an internal combustion engine. The four-stroke petrol engine works in four steps: intake (piston goes down, drawing in air and fuel), compression (piston rises and squeezes the mixture), power (the spark plug ignites it and the explosion pushes the piston down) and exhaust (the piston rises and pushes burnt gases out). Main parts: cylinder, piston, connecting rod, crankshaft, valves, spark plug, carburettor or fuel injector and the cooling and lubrication systems.

A diesel engine has no spark plug; the air is compressed so much it becomes hot enough to ignite injected diesel. Many small generators and motorcycles use a two-stroke or small four-stroke engine.

Safety: always run petrol generators outdoors, well away from windows and doors, because the exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Store fuel away from fire in proper containers and refuel only when the engine is off and cool.

Maintenance: change engine oil regularly, clean the air filter, check coolant, tyre pressure and the spark plug. Regular maintenance saves fuel and avoids breakdowns.

Activity: Draw the four strokes of an engine in order.

lessons.title: Maintenance, Costing and Careers in Technology
lessons.content:
# Maintenance, Costing and Careers in Technology

Maintenance is keeping tools, machines and buildings in good working order. Preventive maintenance is regular care such as cleaning, oiling and checking before a fault occurs. Corrective maintenance is repair after a fault. Good maintenance saves money, time and lives.

Before making a product we cost it. Total cost = materials + labour (+ other costs). Worked example: To make a wooden stool, wood costs ₦3,500, nails ₦300, varnish ₦700 and sandpaper ₦200, so materials = ₦4,700. Labour is ₦2,000, so cost = ₦6,700. To make a profit of 25% on cost: profit = 25% of 6,700 = ₦1,675, selling price = 6,700 + 1,675 = ₦8,375.

Careers in technology include carpenter, bricklayer, welder, plumber, electrician, mechanic, draughtsman, civil engineer, architect and ICT technician. Young Nigerians can learn a trade through apprenticeship, technical colleges and polytechnics, and many start small businesses. Skill, honesty and safety make a good technician.

Practice: A table costs ₦5,000 in materials and ₦2,500 in labour. Find the selling price with 20% profit on cost.

lessons.title: What Is a Computer?
lessons.content:
# What Is a Computer?

A computer is an electronic machine that accepts data (input), processes it by following instructions, stores it, and produces information (output). Data are raw facts and figures, such as the marks 45, 60 and 72. Information is data that has been processed to be useful, such as the class average of 59. The four basic operations are input, processing, storage and output.

Characteristics: speed (millions of operations per second), accuracy (errors usually come from wrong input, not the machine), diligence (it does not tire), versatility (the same computer can write letters, play music and manage accounts) and storage (it can keep huge amounts of information). A computer cannot think for itself; it only follows the instructions in programs.

Example: In a school, student names and scores are data. The computer processes them to print result sheets, which is information.

Activity: Name five places in your community where computers are used and say what task each performs.

lessons.title: Brief History and Generations of Computers
lessons.content:
# Brief History and Generations of Computers

Early calculating tools include the abacus (used in ancient times for counting), Napier's bones, and the Pascaline, a mechanical adding machine built by Blaise Pascal in 1642. In the 1830s Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a machine with ideas that appear in modern computers, and Ada Lovelace wrote notes on how it could be programmed. The first large electronic computer, ENIAC, was unveiled in 1946 and filled a large room.

Generations: First generation (1940s to 1950s) used vacuum tubes and were huge, hot and costly. Second generation (1950s to 1960s) used transistors and were smaller and more reliable. Third generation (1960s to 1970s) used integrated circuits (many transistors on one chip). Fourth generation (from the 1970s) uses microprocessors, which made personal computers possible. The fifth generation is associated with artificial intelligence and advanced networking.

Each generation was smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable than the one before.

Activity: Make a timeline of computer development with five important dates.

lessons.title: Types of Computers
lessons.content:
# Types of Computers

By size and power: supercomputers are the fastest and are used for weather forecasting and scientific research; mainframe computers serve many users at once in banks and large organisations; minicomputers are smaller servers; microcomputers are the personal computers we use daily, including desktops, laptops, tablets and smartphones.

By the way they process data: analogue computers measure continuous quantities such as temperature or speed, as in a petrol pump or a thermometer; digital computers process data as numbers using the binary digits 0 and 1; hybrid computers combine both, as in hospital monitors. By purpose: general-purpose computers do many tasks, while special-purpose computers do one job, such as an ATM or a calculator.

Portable computers such as laptops and tablets can be carried and run on batteries, which is useful where electricity is unreliable.

Activity: Take a list of ten devices around you and say whether each is a computer.

lessons.title: Input Devices
lessons.content:
# Input Devices

Input devices send data and instructions into the computer. The keyboard enters text and numbers. The mouse moves a pointer and selects items. A touchscreen lets you tap and swipe on the display. A scanner converts paper documents and photographs into digital images. A microphone records sound. A webcam captures video. A barcode reader reads the lines on products in supermarkets. A light pen, graphics tablet and joystick are other examples. Biometric readers such as fingerprint scanners are used for attendance and security.

Choosing a device depends on the work. Typing needs a keyboard; drawing is easier with a graphics tablet; scanning documents needs a scanner. Keep the device clean and handle it gently.

Example: At a supermarket till, the barcode reader reads the product code and the computer looks up the price.

Activity: Match each input device to a task: keyboard, scanner, microphone, mouse.

lessons.title: Output Devices
lessons.content:
# Output Devices

Output devices present processed information. The monitor (screen) displays text, pictures and video and gives soft copy, which exists only on the screen or in the computer. The printer prints on paper and gives hard copy; inkjet printers spray ink, laser printers use toner and are faster. Speakers and headphones output sound. A projector shows the screen display on a wall for a class. A plotter prints large drawings.

Some devices do both input and output, such as a touchscreen and a modem. Monitor sizes are measured diagonally in inches. Resolution tells how sharp the picture is.

Example: A student types an essay (input) and reads it on the monitor (soft copy), then prints it (hard copy).

Activity: List the output devices at home and say what each outputs.

lessons.title: Inside the System Unit: CPU, Memory and Ports
lessons.content:
# Inside the System Unit: CPU, Memory and Ports

The system unit is the box that holds the main parts of the computer. The motherboard is the main circuit board to which everything connects. The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the brain of the computer. It has the Control Unit (directs operations), the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU, does calculations and comparisons) and registers (very fast temporary storage). The speed of a CPU is measured in gigahertz (GHz).

Memory: RAM (Random Access Memory) holds the programs and data being used now; it is fast but volatile, which means it loses its contents when power goes off. ROM (Read Only Memory) holds start-up instructions permanently. Other parts are the power supply (changes mains power to low voltage), the cooling fan and storage drive.

Ports are sockets for connecting devices: USB ports (flash drives, keyboards, phones), HDMI (display), audio jacks, Ethernet (network) and the power port.

Activity: Look at a desktop computer or photograph and name every port you can find.

lessons.title: Storage Devices and Units of Memory
lessons.content:
# Storage Devices and Units of Memory

Primary storage is the computer's main memory (RAM and ROM). Secondary storage keeps data permanently: hard disk drives (HDD, magnetic, large and cheap), solid state drives (SSD, faster, no moving parts), flash drives (small and portable), memory cards, CDs and DVDs, and cloud storage, which keeps files on servers on the Internet.

Units: a bit is a single 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits and stores one character. 1 kilobyte (KB) = 1,024 bytes; 1 megabyte (MB) = 1,024 KB; 1 gigabyte (GB) = 1,024 MB; 1 terabyte (TB) = 1,024 GB.

Worked example 1: How many 4 MB photos fit on a 2 GB flash drive? 2 GB = 2 × 1,024 = 2,048 MB. 2,048 ÷ 4 = 512 photos.

Worked example 2: A 700 MB CD holds how many 5 MB songs? 700 ÷ 5 = 140 songs.

Always keep backups of important files on a second device or in the cloud, because storage devices can fail.

Practice: How many 8 MB videos fit on a 4 GB memory card?

lessons.title: Computer Software
lessons.content:
# Computer Software

Software is the set of programs and instructions that tell the hardware what to do. Hardware is the physical parts you can touch. System software controls the computer: the operating system (such as Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS) manages memory, files, devices and the user interface; utility programs include antivirus and disk cleanup. Application software helps users do tasks: word processors, spreadsheets, presentation software, browsers, games, graphics programs and school management software.

Programs are written by programmers using programming languages such as Python, Java or JavaScript. Software may be proprietary (paid, with a licence), free, or open source, where the code is open for others to study and improve. Only install software from trusted sources and keep it updated.

Example: Android on a phone is system software; WhatsApp on that phone is application software.

Activity: List five application programs you use and say what each does.

lessons.title: Care of Computers and Safe Use
lessons.content:
# Care of Computers and Safe Use

A computer is a costly tool and needs care. Keep it in a clean, dry, ventilated room, away from direct sunlight, dust and liquids. Do not eat or drink near it. Switch off properly by using the shut-down command, never by pulling the plug. Use a stabiliser or surge protector against sudden changes in voltage, and where power is unstable use an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) to avoid losing data. Do not open the system unit unless you are trained.

Health: sit upright with your feet flat, your eyes level with the top of the screen about an arm's length away, and your wrists straight when typing. Take a break every 30 minutes to rest your eyes and stretch. Avoid very bright screens in a dark room.

Clean the screen with a soft dry cloth and the keyboard with a soft brush. Handle disks and flash drives gently and never remove a flash drive while it is copying.

Activity: Write five rules for your school computer room.

# The Desktop and Operating System Basics

To start a computer, press the power button and wait for the operating system to load, then sign in if needed. The first screen is the desktop. It has icons (small pictures that stand for programs, files and folders), the taskbar (a bar along the bottom showing running programs and the clock) and the Start menu, from which programs are opened. A program runs in a window that can be minimised, maximised or closed with the buttons in the top corner.

The operating system also gives you settings to change the background, volume, date and time, and network connection. To shut down, use the Start menu and choose Shut down; to leave the computer for a short time you can choose Sleep or Lock.

Example: Click the Start button, find the calculator program and click on it. A window opens. Click the X button to close it.

lessons.title: Files and Folders
lessons.content:
# Files and Folders

A file is a collection of data stored under a name, such as a letter, a photograph or a song. A folder (or directory) is a container used to organise files. Folders can hold other folders (subfolders). Give files short, clear names such as English_Essay_Term1 so that you can find them later.

File extensions show the type of file: .docx for Word documents, .xlsx for spreadsheets, .pptx for presentations, .pdf for portable documents, .jpg and .png for pictures, .mp3 for audio and .mp4 for video.

Common operations: create a new folder (right-click, then New, then Folder), rename, copy (make a duplicate), move (cut and paste), and delete (sent to the Recycle Bin, from which it can be restored until the bin is emptied). Always keep a copy of important files on another storage device.

Example: A student makes a folder named JSS1, with subfolders for English, Maths and Science, and saves each subject's work in its own folder.

lessons.content:
# The Keyboard

The keyboard has several areas. The alphanumeric keys include letters, numbers and punctuation. The function keys F1 to F12 at the top do special tasks. The numeric keypad on the right is for fast number entry. The navigation keys (arrows, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down) move the cursor. Special keys: Enter (new line or accept), Space bar, Backspace (delete to the left), Delete (delete to the right), Shift (capital letters and symbols), Caps Lock, Tab, Ctrl, Alt and Esc.

Touch typing means typing without looking at the keys. Place your fingers on the home row: A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right hand, with the thumbs on the space bar. The keys F and J have small raised marks to help you find the place. Practise regularly and keep your wrists straight.

Useful shortcuts: Ctrl + C (copy), Ctrl + X (cut), Ctrl + V (paste), Ctrl + Z (undo), Ctrl + S (save), Ctrl + P (print) and Ctrl + A (select all).

Activity: Type the sentence The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog five times without looking at the keys.

# Using the Mouse and Touchscreen

A mouse has a left button, a right button and often a scroll wheel. Click means press the left button once to select. Double-click means press twice quickly to open. Right-click opens a menu of options for the item under the pointer. Drag and drop means holding the left button down, moving an item and releasing it where you want. The scroll wheel moves the page up and down.

On a touchscreen, the main gestures are tap (select), double tap, long press (open options), swipe (scroll or move), and pinch or spread (zoom out or in). Keep your fingers and the screen clean.

A laptop has a touchpad that works like a mouse. Slide a finger to move the pointer and tap to click. To avoid mistakes, move slowly and look at where the pointer is.

lessons.content:
# Word Processing: Creating a Document

A word processor is a program for writing and formatting text. Examples are Microsoft Word, Google Docs and LibreOffice Writer. To make a document, open the program, choose a blank document and start typing. Do not press Enter at the end of every line; the text wraps automatically. Press Enter only to start a new paragraph.

Formatting changes the appearance of text: bold (B) for emphasis, italic (I), underline (U), font type, font size and colour, and alignment (left, centre, right and justified). To format, first select the text by dragging over it, then apply the format.

Save regularly: choose File then Save As, name your file and choose a folder. Use Ctrl + S as you work so you will not lose it if power fails. To print, choose File then Print, choose the printer and the number of copies, and click Print.

Example: A student types a letter to her teacher, centres the title in bold 16 point, writes the paragraphs in 12 point and saves the file in the English folder.

Activity: Type a short paragraph about your school, make the title bold and centred and save it as My_School.

lessons.title: Editing and Page Layout
lessons.content:
# Editing and Page Layout

Editing means changing and improving a document. Basic edits: cut (remove and keep), copy (duplicate) and paste (insert). Undo reverses the last action and Redo restores it. Find and Replace locates a word and changes it everywhere. The spell checker underlines misspelt words in red and grammar issues in blue; always read your work yourself too, because the checker cannot catch every mistake.

Page layout: margins are the blank spaces round the edges (usually about 2.5 cm), orientation can be portrait (upright) or landscape (sideways), and paper size is usually A4. Line spacing controls the space between lines. Lists can be bulleted or numbered; insert a table to organise information in rows and columns.

Headers and footers appear at the top and bottom of every page, such as the page number or school name.

Practice: Open a document and use Find and Replace to change 'teh' to 'the'. Then change the page to landscape and add page numbers.

# Presentation Software

Presentation software such as PowerPoint, Google Slides or Impress is used to prepare slides that support a talk. Each slide holds text, pictures, charts, sounds or video. Choose a layout, such as a title slide or a title with content, and add a theme (design) to give the whole show a consistent look.

Good practice: use a short title, a few short points (not full paragraphs), large, readable fonts (at least 24 point), strong contrast between text and background and no more than one main idea per slide. Pictures should be clear and relevant. Use transitions and animations sparingly because too many distract the audience.

To run the show press F5 or choose Slide Show, then use the arrow keys to move between slides and Esc to end it. Practise speaking before presenting, and do not just read from the screen.

lessons.title: Spreadsheets
lessons.content:
# Spreadsheets

A spreadsheet is a program for working with numbers and calculations. Examples are Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc. The screen is a grid of columns (labelled A, B, C...) and rows (numbered 1, 2, 3...). Where a column and a row meet is a cell, named by its address; the cell in column B and row 3 is B3. A group of cells is a range, written B2:B6.

Formulas begin with an equals sign. =A1+B1 adds two cells. =SUM(B2:B6) adds all the cells from B2 to B6. =AVERAGE(B2:B6) finds the average. The result changes automatically if you change the numbers.

Worked example: Marks for a student are in cells B2, B3 and B4: 45, 60 and 72. The total is =SUM(B2:B4) = 177. The average is =AVERAGE(B2:B4) = 177 ÷ 3 = 59.

You can also make charts, such as a bar chart, from selected data. Always label the columns clearly.

Practice: Record five test scores and calculate their total and average.

# Using Mobile Devices and Apps

A smartphone or tablet is a small computer that runs an operating system (Android or iOS) and apps. Apps are installed from official stores such as Google Play and the App Store. Before installing, read what permissions an app asks for. A calculator app should not need access to your contacts.

Keep the device updated, protect it with a screen lock (PIN, pattern or fingerprint), and keep enough free storage by deleting unused apps and files. Charge using the right charger and do not use the phone while charging in a way that makes it very hot. Use data or Wi-Fi sensibly because data costs money.

Learning apps, dictionaries, calculators, maps and note-taking apps can help your studies. Use the phone responsibly in class: only when the teacher allows. Switch it off or on silent during lessons and examinations.

lessons.title: Data and Information Processing
lessons.content:
# Data and Information Processing

Information processing is the series of steps that turn raw data into useful information. The stages are: collecting data, entering it, processing it (sorting, calculating, comparing), storing it and outputting the results. This is often called the information processing cycle.

Example: A school collects scores from teachers (data collection), types them into a spreadsheet (input), calculates totals, averages and positions (processing), saves the file (storage) and prints report cards (output).

Information should be accurate, up to date, complete, relevant and delivered on time. Poor data causes poor decisions. The saying garbage in, garbage out means that if wrong data goes in, wrong results come out.

Manual information systems use paper registers and files; electronic systems use computers. Electronic systems store more, work faster and find records quickly, but need electricity, security and trained users.

Activity: Describe how a shop might process daily sales using a computer.

lessons.title: Computer Networks
lessons.content:
# Computer Networks

A computer network is a group of computers and devices connected so they can share information and resources such as files, printers and an Internet connection. Types: a LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small area like a school computer room or office; a MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) covers a city; a WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a large area such as a country, and the Internet is the largest WAN.

Network devices: a switch connects computers in a LAN; a router connects networks together and sends data to the right place; a modem converts signals so a computer can use a telephone or fibre line; a network interface card connects a computer to the network. Connections can be wired (Ethernet cable) or wireless (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth).

Advantages: sharing of files and devices, easy communication and central backup. Disadvantages: security risks, viruses spreading quickly and breakdown of the main server affecting all users.

Activity: Draw a simple diagram of a school LAN with a router, switch, five computers and a printer.

lessons.content:
# The Internet and the World Wide Web

The Internet is a worldwide network of networks. The World Wide Web (WWW) is the collection of web pages and websites that we access through the Internet. They are not the same: the Internet is the network, and the web is a service that runs on it. Email, video calls and online games also use the Internet.

To access the web, you need a device, an Internet connection from an Internet Service Provider (ISP) and a web browser such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari or Edge. Every website has a URL (web address), for example www.example.com.ng. In the address, the last parts show the type or country: .com (commercial), .org (organisation), .edu (education), .gov (government) and .ng (Nigeria), as in .edu.ng for Nigerian educational institutions and .gov.ng for government.

A web page is a single document; a website is a group of related pages; a home page is the first page. Links (hyperlinks) take you from one page to another.

lessons.content:
# Email and Online Communication

Electronic mail (email) is a message sent from one person to another over the Internet. An email address has the form name@domain, such as ada.obi@example.com. The part before @ is the user name and the part after is the mail service. To send a message, click Compose or New, type the receiver's address in To, a short clear Subject, and then the message. Cc sends a copy to another person who can be seen by all, and Bcc sends a hidden copy. An attachment is a file sent with the message. Sent messages are in the Sent folder, and incoming ones are in the Inbox.

Email etiquette: use a polite greeting and closing, be brief and clear, check spelling, never type in capitals only because it looks like shouting, and think before you send. Do not open attachments from unknown senders because they may contain viruses. Keep your password secret.

Other tools: instant messaging, video calls and online classrooms. Use them respectfully, and only chat with people you know.

Practice: Write an email to your teacher asking for a copy of the class notes. Include a subject, greeting and closing.

lessons.content:
# Searching and Evaluating Information Online

A search engine such as Google or Bing finds web pages containing the words you type. Choose keywords carefully: use a few specific words rather than a whole sentence, such as causes of malaria Nigeria. Put exact phrases in quotation marks. Use the Images, News or Maps tabs for other results. Look beyond the first result.

Not everything online is true. To judge whether a source can be trusted, ask: Who wrote it? Is the author an expert or organisation? When was it published? Is it supported by evidence and other reliable sources? Is the website trying to sell something or promote a view? Government, university and established news sites are usually more reliable than anonymous posts. Be careful with viral messages and always confirm important information in at least two reliable places.

When you use information in a project, write it in your own words and list your source. Copying someone's work without crediting it is plagiarism.

lessons.title: Staying Safe Online
lessons.content:
# Staying Safe Online

The Internet is useful but has dangers. Phishing messages pretend to come from a bank or company and try to trick you into giving passwords, PINs or one-time passwords (OTPs). Scams promise money, prizes or jobs if you pay first. Cyberbullying is using messages or posts to harass someone. Strangers may pretend to be friends.

Protect yourself: use strong passwords of at least twelve characters mixing letters, numbers and symbols, and a different password for each account; never share passwords, PINs or OTPs; do not click links in strange messages; keep personal details such as address and school private; think before posting because online posts last; and switch on two-step verification when it is available.

Report cyberbullying and threats to a parent, teacher or trusted adult. In Nigeria, the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act of 2015, since amended, makes offences such as online fraud, identity theft and cyberstalking punishable by law.

Activity: Make a poster with five rules for staying safe online.

lessons.title: Computer Viruses and Protection
lessons.content:
# Computer Viruses and Protection

Malware is harmful software designed to damage or steal. A computer virus attaches itself to files and spreads when they are copied. A worm spreads by itself through networks. A trojan pretends to be a useful program. Spyware secretly records activity. Ransomware locks files and demands payment.

Viruses spread through infected flash drives, email attachments, unsafe downloads and dubious websites. Signs of infection include slow performance, strange pop-ups, programs that open by themselves and missing files.

Protection: install a reliable antivirus and keep it updated; update the operating system; scan flash drives before opening files; download programs only from official sources; do not open suspicious attachments; use backups so that files can be recovered; and log out from shared computers.

Example: A student copies a project from a friend's flash drive without scanning it, and the virus deletes his files. If he had scanned it and kept a backup, he would have lost nothing.

Activity: Check whether the computers in your school have antivirus software and note when it was last updated.

lessons.title: Computers in Society
lessons.content:
# Computers in Society

Computers are used in almost every area of life. In education: online lessons, digital libraries and results processing. In banking: ATMs, point-of-sale (POS) machines, internet banking and mobile money. In healthcare: patient records, scanning machines and telemedicine. In agriculture: weather data, market prices and farm records. In transport: ticketing, tracking and traffic control. In offices: documents, accounts and communication. In entertainment: films, music and games. Nigerian businesses, farmers, traders and students use phones daily.

Benefits: speed, accuracy, access to information, new jobs and business opportunities. Concerns: loss of some manual jobs, cost, health problems from overuse, loss of privacy, cybercrime and the digital divide, where some people have more access to technology than others, because of cost, electricity or location.

Use technology responsibly, and use it to solve real problems in your community.

lessons.title: Algorithms and Flowcharts
lessons.content:
# Algorithms and Flowcharts

An algorithm is a step-by-step list of instructions for solving a problem. Computers need exact and complete instructions, so we plan with algorithms before writing programs. A good algorithm is clear, ordered, finite and produces the correct result.

Example (everyday): to make tea: 1. Boil water. 2. Put a tea bag in a cup. 3. Pour in the water. 4. Wait three minutes. 5. Remove the tea bag. 6. Add sugar and milk if wanted.

A flowchart is a diagram of an algorithm using symbols: an oval for start and end; a parallelogram for input and output; a rectangle for a process or calculation; a diamond for a decision with yes and no paths; and arrows showing the direction of flow.

Worked example: Find the larger of two numbers. Start; input A; input B; decision: is A greater than B? If yes, output A; if no, output B; end. Try it with A = 8 and B = 5. The answer is 8.

Computers store everything in binary, using only 0 and 1. Programs written in languages such as Python are translated into binary so the processor can run them.

Practice: Write an algorithm for withdrawing money from an ATM, then draw its flowchart.

lessons.title: Needs, Wants, Goods and Services
lessons.content:
# Needs, Wants, Goods and Services

People have needs and wants. Needs are things we must have to survive: food, clothing, shelter and clean water. Wants are things we would like to have but can live without, such as a new phone or fashionable shoes. Because resources are limited and wants are unlimited, people must choose, and every choice has an opportunity cost: the next best thing we give up.

Goods are physical things we can touch, such as bread, shoes and books. Services are activities done for us, such as teaching, haircutting, banking and transport. Business is the activity of producing or selling goods and services to satisfy needs and to make a profit.

Business activities are grouped into industry (producing goods), commerce (the buying and selling of goods and the services that help it, such as transport and banking) and direct services (teachers, doctors, hairdressers).

Example: A student has ₦1,000 and wants both a notebook (a need) and a snack (a want). Choosing the notebook means giving up the snack; the snack is the opportunity cost.

Activity: List five needs and five wants of a Nigerian family.

lessons.title: Production and Factors of Production
lessons.content:
# Production and Factors of Production

Production is the making of goods and services that satisfy wants. Primary production extracts raw materials directly from nature: farming, fishing, mining, logging and oil drilling. Secondary production changes raw materials into finished goods: baking bread from flour, making furniture, refining oil. Tertiary production provides services such as trade, banking, transport and teaching.

Four factors of production are needed. Land includes all natural resources: soil, water, minerals, forests, crude oil; its reward is rent. Labour is human effort, physical and mental; its reward is wages or salary. Capital is man-made resources used to produce more goods, such as machines, tools and money for business; its reward is interest. The entrepreneur organises the other three and takes the risk; the reward is profit.

Example: A baker needs land for the shop, labour in the helpers, capital in the oven and flour, and the owner who organises and risks the business.

Activity: Identify the four factors in a local tailoring business.

lessons.title: Trade: Home and Foreign, Wholesale and Retail
lessons.content:
# Trade: Home and Foreign, Wholesale and Retail

Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services. Home (internal) trade takes place within a country, while foreign (external) trade takes place between countries. Goods sold abroad are exports and goods bought from abroad are imports. Nigeria has long exported crude oil, cocoa, sesame and other products, and imports machines, vehicles and many manufactured items.

Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities from producers and sell in smaller quantities to retailers. Retailers buy from wholesalers and sell in small quantities to the final consumer. This chain of distribution is producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer. Examples of retail outlets are market stalls, kiosks, supermarkets and online shops. Market days are important in many Nigerian communities.

Wholesalers help producers by storing goods, giving credit to retailers and breaking bulk. Retailers help consumers by stocking different brands and offering convenience and advice.

Example: A cocoa farmer sells to a buyer, who sells to an exporter; the exporter ships to another country. This is foreign trade.

Activity: Visit a local market and list five wholesalers and five retailers.

lessons.title: Forms of Business Ownership
lessons.content:
# Forms of Business Ownership

A sole proprietorship is owned and run by one person, such as a roadside trader or a tailor. It is easy to start and the owner keeps all profit, but the owner has unlimited liability, so personal property can be used to pay debts, and raising money is hard. A partnership is a business owned by two or more people (generally up to twenty) who share profits and risk, usually under a partnership agreement; disagreement and unlimited liability are risks.

A limited liability company is a separate legal person registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC). The owners (shareholders) are liable only up to the money they put in. It can raise large sums by selling shares but must follow stricter rules and file returns. A private company cannot sell shares to the public; a public company can.

A cooperative society is formed by people who join to help each other, for example farmers who market produce together or workers who save together. Profits are shared according to the members' use of the society's services. Business names should be registered with the CAC.

Activity: Name one local business of each type and state one advantage of its form of ownership.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship
lessons.content:
# Entrepreneurship

An entrepreneur is a person who identifies a need, organises resources and takes the risk of starting a business to meet it. Qualities of good entrepreneurs include creativity, hard work, honesty, discipline, willingness to take sensible risks, good communication, determination to continue after failure and ability to manage money and people.

Steps in starting a small business: find a problem or need; research the market and customers; make a simple business plan with the product, costs and expected income; raise start-up money from savings, family or loans; register the business; set up and promote it; and keep records. Many Nigerians run small businesses such as food vending, tailoring, phone repair, poultry and online selling.

Benefits of entrepreneurship: it creates jobs, reduces poverty, brings new products and raises the standard of living. Challenges include lack of capital, unstable electricity, high costs, poor roads, competition and insecurity.

Example: A student who sees that classmates need printed notes buys a printer and starts a small school printing service.

Activity: Write a one-page plan for a small business you could start near your school.

lessons.title: Money and Its Functions
lessons.content:
# Money and Its Functions

Before money, people used barter, exchanging goods directly, for example yams for fish. Barter has problems: you must find someone who wants what you have (double coincidence of wants), it is hard to divide goods and to store value. Later people used items such as cowries, manilla, salt and beads as money. Today we use coins, notes and electronic money.

Functions of money: a medium of exchange (we use it to buy), a unit of account (it measures the value of goods), a store of value (it keeps value over time) and a standard for deferred payment (we can owe and repay later). Good money is acceptable, durable, portable, divisible, scarce and stable in value.

The naira became Nigeria's currency in 1973. The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) issues it, controls its supply and regulates banks. Handle money with care, and report counterfeit notes to the police or bank. Inflation is a general rise in prices, which reduces what a naira can buy.

Example: With the naira, a trader can sell yams and use the money to buy fish later. The naira acts as a medium of exchange and a store of value.

Activity: Imagine you must trade a goat for a haircut by barter. Describe three difficulties.

lessons.title: Banking
lessons.content:
# Banking

A bank is an institution that keeps people's money safe, gives loans and offers payment services. Types of banks: the central bank (CBN) regulates the system; commercial banks serve the public and businesses; microfinance banks give small loans and savings services to small traders and low-income earners; development banks and mortgage banks lend for industry and housing.

Accounts: a savings account earns interest and suits regular savers; a current account is used for frequent payments and cheques; a fixed deposit holds a large sum for an agreed time to earn higher interest. Services: deposits and withdrawals, transfers, ATMs, debit cards, mobile banking, POS and loans. Deposits in licensed banks are insured by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) up to a limit.

To open an account you usually need identification and a Bank Verification Number (BVN). Never share your PIN, password, card number or OTP with anyone, even someone claiming to be from the bank.

Worked example: A savings account pays 4% interest per year. On ₦25,000 for one year the interest is 4/100 × 25,000 = ₦1,000.

Activity: Visit a bank and collect an account opening form.

lessons.title: Advertising and Marketing
lessons.content:
# Advertising and Marketing

Marketing is everything a business does to find out what customers want and to get products to them. Advertising is a way of telling people about products to persuade them to buy. Media of advertising include radio, television, newspapers, posters and billboards, handbills, social media and word of mouth. The best medium depends on the target audience and the cost.

The marketing mix is the 4 Ps: Product (what is sold and its quality), Price (what the customer pays), Place (where and how it is sold) and Promotion (how people learn about it). A good business studies customers, sets a fair price, makes the product easy to find and promotes it honestly.

Advertising should be truthful. False claims mislead customers and can lead to punishment by regulators. Advantages: it informs, helps competition and creates jobs. Disadvantages: it costs money, which can raise prices, and it may persuade people to buy what they do not need.

Activity: Design a poster to advertise a school snack stall using the 4 Ps.

lessons.title: Aids to Trade
lessons.content:
# Aids to Trade

Aids to trade are services that make buying and selling easier. Transport moves goods from producers to consumers by road, rail, water and air. Warehousing stores goods until they are needed and keeps them safe. Banking provides safe keeping, loans and payment methods. Insurance protects against loss from fire, theft and accidents for a small payment called a premium. Communication (post, phone, internet) links buyers and sellers. Advertising informs customers.

Without these aids, trade would be slow and risky. A farmer in the north could not sell tomatoes in the south without transport, storage, communication and payment.

Challenges: poor roads, delays at ports, high transport costs and poor storage cause losses. Good infrastructure improves trade and lowers prices.

Worked example: A trader pays an insurance premium of ₦2,000 on goods worth ₦200,000. When a fire destroys the goods, the insurance company compensates the loss, so the trader loses only the small premium.

Activity: Explain how transport, banking and communication help a trader selling yams in a distant town.

lessons.content:
# The Office and Its Functions

An office is a place where the administrative and clerical work of an organisation is done. Offices may be in a school, bank, hospital, company or government ministry. The main functions are receiving and giving information, keeping records, handling money and documents, and supporting other departments.

Types of offices include the private office of a manager, the general open office where many staff share a room, and the home or virtual office. Office staff include the manager, secretary, clerks, typists, receptionists, messengers and cleaners. Each has duties: the receptionist welcomes visitors, the secretary handles the manager's correspondence and appointments, the clerk keeps records and the messenger delivers documents.

A good office is clean, orderly, well lit and ventilated, with safe electrical wiring and a fire extinguisher. Staff should be punctual, honest, courteous and keep company information confidential.

lessons.title: Office Machines and Equipment
lessons.content:
# Office Machines and Equipment

Modern offices use many machines. The computer is used for typing, calculating, storing records and communicating. The printer produces hard copies and the scanner converts documents to digital files. The photocopier makes copies of documents. The telephone and the intercom link staff and the outside world. The shredder destroys confidential papers. The stapler, punch and paper clips hold documents. The calculator does quick arithmetic and the fax is an older machine for sending documents by phone line. Power backup devices such as inverters and UPS keep machines working when there is a power cut.

Care of equipment: read instructions, switch off when not in use, clean regularly, keep liquids away, report faults and have machines serviced. Never force paper into a jammed machine; switch it off first.

Example: A secretary types a letter on a computer (word processing), prints it, photocopies it for the file and scans it for emailing.

Activity: Choose a machine and write three rules for its safe use.

lessons.title: Office Furniture and Stationery
lessons.content:
# Office Furniture and Stationery

Furniture includes desks, chairs, filing cabinets, shelves, notice boards and cupboards. Choose furniture that is comfortable and safe; an adjustable chair with a good back support helps prevent back pain. Arrange furniture to give enough space to move and to keep exits free.

Stationery is the materials used in office writing and recording: paper, envelopes, pens, pencils, notebooks, folders, files, rubber stamps and ink pads, rulers, erasers, glue and tape. Consumable stationery is used up and replaced often, while equipment such as staplers lasts longer.

Stock control keeps enough supplies without wasting money. The store-keeper records items received and issued. A requisition is a written request for supplies from a department, signed by an authorised person. Items are issued only against a requisition.

Worked example: A school office uses 12 boxes of pens in a term, and needs 20% extra as a reserve. 20% of 12 = 2.4, so order about 15 boxes.

Activity: Prepare a requisition for ten files, two reams of paper and five pens.

lessons.title: Filing and Records
lessons.content:
# Filing and Records

Filing means arranging documents in an agreed order so that they can be found quickly. Records are kept in files, folders, cabinets and, increasingly, on computers. Good filing saves time, protects important papers and gives proof of past actions.

Methods of filing: alphabetical (by name), numerical (by number), geographical (by place), chronological (by date) and by subject. Alphabetical filing is the most common. Rules: arrange by the surname first, then the first name. Mr. Ade Bello is filed as Bello, Ade. If surnames are the same, use first names.

Worked example: Arrange alphabetically Okafor, Adamu, Eze, Bello. The correct order is Adamu, Bello, Eze, Okafor.

Rules for good filing: remove pins and clips, place the newest paper on top, keep a record of files taken out (a file movement record), do not overfill folders and keep confidential files locked. On a computer, name files clearly, sort them into folders and back them up.

Practice: Arrange alphabetically: Yusuf, Nwosu, Balogun, Danjuma, Adeyemi.

lessons.title: Business Letters
lessons.content:
# Business Letters

A business letter is a formal written message to a person or organisation. Its parts: the sender's address, the date, the receiver's name and address, the salutation (Dear Sir, Dear Madam or Dear Mr Bello), the subject heading, the body, the complimentary close, the signature and the sender's name and position.

If the letter begins Dear Sir or Dear Madam, close with Yours faithfully. If it begins with a name, such as Dear Mr Bello, close with Yours sincerely. The body states the purpose in a clear opening, gives details in the middle and ends with the action expected. Use polite, direct language and correct spelling, and keep paragraphs short.

Example of a subject heading: APPLICATION FOR A SCHOLARSHIP. A request, an order, a complaint, an application and an invitation are common letters.

Layout styles: in the fully blocked style all lines start at the left margin; in the semi-blocked style paragraphs are indented. Type on one side of the paper and leave a margin.

Activity: Write a letter to a bookshop ordering twenty exercise books and asking for the price.

lessons.content:
# Using the Telephone

Telephone manners reflect the image of the business. When answering: pick up quickly (within three rings), greet politely, state the name of the organisation and your name, listen carefully, speak clearly and calmly, and ask how you can help. If you must put a caller on hold, ask permission and return soon. Never shout, eat or chew while on the phone.

Taking a message: record the date and time, the caller's name, number and organisation, the person the message is for, the message and your name. Repeat the details to be sure. Pass the message on promptly. When making a call, plan what you will say, have pen and paper ready, identify yourself and end politely.

Mobile phones should be switched to silent in meetings and classes. Do not share a caller's details with others.

Practice: Role-play a call in which a customer asks to speak to the manager, who is out. Take a message.

# Reception and Visitors

The receptionist is the first person visitors meet, so the office image depends on this person. Duties: welcome visitors warmly, find out their name and purpose, check appointments, inform the person to be visited, direct visitors to the waiting area, keep a visitors' book recording names, times in and out and who was visited, and handle phone calls and mail.

An appointment is an arrangement to meet at a set time. Use an appointment diary or calendar. Confirm appointments in advance and avoid clashes. If an executive is not available, offer another time politely and never promise what you cannot deliver.

A receptionist should be neatly dressed, smiling, patient and tactful, and should keep confidential matters private. Security matters: do not allow unknown people into restricted areas.

lessons.title: Handling Mail and Postal Services
lessons.content:
# Handling Mail and Postal Services

Mail is the letters, parcels and packages sent and received by an organisation. Incoming mail procedure: receive, sort, open (except marked private or confidential), date-stamp, record in the incoming mail register, and deliver to the right person promptly. Outgoing mail: write the letter, make a copy for the file, address the envelope correctly, record in the outgoing mail register and post.

The Nigerian Postal Service (NIPOST) provides services such as ordinary mail, registered mail (with proof of posting and delivery), speed post and parcels. Private courier companies provide fast delivery of documents and parcels. Email has replaced many letters, but official or legal documents are still posted.

An envelope should have the receiver's full name and address clearly written, the postcode, and a stamp (or the correct postage). Put your return address on the back.

Activity: Address an envelope to your school's principal and write down the steps of handling incoming mail.

lessons.title: Keyboarding and Document Preparation
lessons.content:
# Keyboarding and Document Preparation

Keyboarding is the skill of typing quickly and accurately. A beginner should first learn the home row, practise touch typing and keep correct posture. Speed is measured in words per minute (wpm), where five characters, including spaces, count as one word.

Worked example 1: A student types 300 words in 6 minutes. The speed is 300 ÷ 6 = 50 wpm. Worked example 2 (net speed): The same student made 6 errors. Net words = 300 − 6 = 294, so the net speed is 294 ÷ 6 = 49 wpm. Accuracy matters more than speed in the office.

Documents that an office types include letters, memos (short internal messages), reports, minutes of meetings, notices and tables. Always proofread before printing. Use a clear font such as Times New Roman or Arial in size 11 or 12, with consistent spacing and margins.

Practice: A clerk types 450 words in 9 minutes. Find the speed in wpm.

lessons.title: Book-keeping and Source Documents
lessons.content:
# Book-keeping and Source Documents

Book-keeping is the systematic recording of the financial transactions of a business. It tells the owner how much money came in, how much went out, what is owed and what is owing, and whether the business is making a profit. It is also needed for tax and for loans. Accounts must be neat, accurate and up to date.

Every transaction begins with a source document, which is the proof that it took place. An invoice is sent by the seller to the buyer showing goods supplied, prices and total. A receipt is given as proof of payment. A delivery note accompanies goods and is signed by the receiver. A credit note is issued by a seller when goods are returned or an overcharge is made. A debit note requests additional payment. A cash voucher records small cash payments. A quotation states the price a seller will charge, and an order is a buyer's request for goods.

Example: A shop orders 10 bags of rice. The supplier sends the rice with a delivery note and an invoice. When the shop pays, it receives a receipt.

Activity: Collect a receipt from a shop and list the information it shows.

lessons.title: The Cash Book
lessons.content:
# The Cash Book

The cash book records all money received and paid. It has two sides. The left-hand side (debit) records money received (receipts) and the right-hand side (credit) records money paid out (payments). At the end of a period, add each side, subtract the smaller from the larger to find the balance, and carry it down (balance brought down, b/d) as the opening balance for the next period.

Worked example: Mrs Eze starts the month with ₦20,000 cash. She receives ₦15,000 from sales and ₦5,000 from a customer who owed her. She pays ₦8,000 for shop rent and ₦12,000 for goods. Receipts: 20,000 + 15,000 + 5,000 = ₦40,000. Payments: 8,000 + 12,000 = ₦20,000. Balance carried down: 40,000 − 20,000 = ₦20,000. This balance is the opening cash for next month.

Check: each side of the closing account should add to the same total after the balance is inserted.

Practice: A trader has ₦10,000 cash. He receives ₦7,500 from sales and pays ₦3,000 for transport. Find the closing balance.

lessons.title: The Petty Cash Book
lessons.content:
# The Petty Cash Book

Petty cash is a small amount of cash kept in the office to pay for small expenses such as transport, stationery, postage and refreshments. A person called the petty cashier is in charge. Under the imprest system, a fixed amount, the imprest, is given at the start. When money is spent, a petty cash voucher is signed. At the end of the period the cashier adds up the spending and is given exactly that amount to bring the cash back up to the imprest.

Worked example: The imprest is ₦10,000. During the week the cashier spends ₦2,500 on transport, ₦1,800 on stationery and ₦1,200 on refreshments. Total spent = 2,500 + 1,800 + 1,200 = ₦5,500. Cash left = 10,000 − 5,500 = ₦4,500. The cashier is reimbursed ₦5,500 to restore ₦10,000.

Advantages: it keeps the main cash book from being crowded with small items and saves time. It needs honesty and careful records.

Practice: With an imprest of ₦8,000, a cashier spends ₦3,000 on postage and ₦1,500 on cleaning materials. Find the amount to be reimbursed.

lessons.title: Profit and Loss
lessons.content:
# Profit and Loss

Profit is the amount by which the selling price (SP) is greater than the cost price (CP). Loss is the amount by which the cost price is greater than the selling price. Profit = SP − CP. Loss = CP − SP. Percentage profit = (profit ÷ CP) × 100. Percentage loss = (loss ÷ CP) × 100.

Worked example 1: A trader buys 10 bags of rice at ₦2,000 each and sells all at ₦2,600 each. Cost = ₦20,000, selling = ₦26,000, profit = ₦6,000. Percentage profit = 6,000 ÷ 20,000 × 100 = 30%.

Worked example 2: A bag bought for ₦500 and sold for ₦400 gives a loss of ₦100. Percentage loss = 100 ÷ 500 × 100 = 20%.

Gross profit = sales − cost of goods sold. Net profit = gross profit − expenses. Worked example 3: Sales ₦500,000, cost of goods ₦320,000, expenses ₦60,000. Gross profit = ₦180,000. Net profit = 180,000 − 60,000 = ₦120,000.

Practice: A shirt bought for ₦3,000 is sold for ₦3,600. Find the profit and the percentage profit.

lessons.title: Discounts
lessons.content:
# Discounts

A discount is a reduction in price. A trade discount is deducted from the list price by a seller, usually for buying in bulk, and appears on the invoice. A cash discount is a reduction given for paying promptly or in cash.

Worked example 1: Goods have a list price of ₦8,000 with a 10% trade discount. The discount is 10% of 8,000 = ₦800, so the invoice price is ₦7,200.

Worked example 2: If a further 5% cash discount is allowed for quick payment on the ₦7,200, the discount is 5% of 7,200 = ₦360, so the buyer pays ₦6,840.

Worked example 3: A shop reduces the price of a ₦12,000 bag by 15% in a sale. 15% of 12,000 = ₦1,800, so the sale price is ₦10,200.

Discounts can attract customers, but the seller must make sure that the selling price still covers costs.

Practice: Find the price of a ₦5,000 item after a 20% discount.

lessons.title: Simple Interest and Savings
lessons.content:
# Simple Interest and Savings

Interest is the money paid for the use of someone's money. If you save with a bank, the bank pays you interest. If you borrow, you pay interest. Simple interest is calculated on the original sum only: I = (P × R × T) ÷ 100, where P is the principal (the amount), R is the rate per cent per year and T is the time in years. The amount A = P + I.

Worked example 1: Find the simple interest on ₦50,000 at 5% per year for 2 years. I = 50,000 × 5 × 2 ÷ 100 = ₦5,000. The amount is ₦55,000.

Worked example 2: ₦20,000 earns ₦3,000 in 3 years. Find the rate. R = (100 × I) ÷ (P × T) = (100 × 3,000) ÷ (20,000 × 3) = 5%.

Compound interest adds interest to the principal each year so you earn interest on interest; it grows savings faster. Loans can be costly when interest rates are high, so compare offers.

Practice: Find the interest on ₦30,000 at 4% for 3 years.

lessons.title: Personal Budgeting
lessons.content:
# Personal Budgeting

A budget is a plan for how to use income over a period. Income is the money you receive (allowance, wages, profit). Expenses are the money you spend. A good budget lists fixed needs first, such as school fees, food and transport, then wants, and puts some money into savings. A surplus means income exceeds expenses and a deficit means expenses exceed income.

Worked example: A family's monthly income is ₦30,000. Planned expenses: food ₦12,000, transport ₦6,000, school ₦5,000, savings ₦4,000. Total = 12,000 + 6,000 + 5,000 + 4,000 = ₦27,000. Surplus = 30,000 − 27,000 = ₦3,000.

Tips: record what you spend; plan before you shop; compare prices; avoid buying on credit when you cannot repay; save first; and review your budget each month. A school business such as a tuck shop needs a budget too.

Practice: A student receives ₦5,000 monthly. Plan how to spend it on transport, snacks, books and savings.

lessons.title: Methods of Payment and Consumer Rights
lessons.content:
# Methods of Payment and Consumer Rights

People pay for goods in different ways: cash, cheque, bank transfer, debit card, POS machine, mobile money and online payment. Always get a receipt and check the amount before confirming a payment. When using a transfer or POS, confirm the receiver's name. Protect your PIN and never share your OTP.

Consumers are people who buy and use goods and services. Consumers have rights: the right to safety, to information, to choose, to be heard and to get redress (compensation). In Nigeria, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) works to protect consumers, and NAFDAC checks food and drugs. Check the NAFDAC number, the expiry date and the seller's information before buying packaged products.

Consumers also have responsibilities: to be careful, to ask questions, to complain politely, to keep receipts and not to buy fake or stolen goods.

Activity: Examine a packaged food. Write down the NAFDAC number, manufacturing and expiry dates, and ingredients.

lessons.title: Saving, Borrowing and Financial Safety
lessons.content:
# Saving, Borrowing and Financial Safety

Saving means keeping some income for the future, for emergencies and for goals. Ways of saving include a bank savings account, a cooperative society and traditional rotating savings groups such as ajo or esusu (Yoruba), isusu (Igbo) and adashe (Hausa), in which members contribute a fixed amount regularly and take turns to receive the whole pot. Worked example: 10 members each pay ₦5,000 a week; the pot is 10 × 5,000 = ₦50,000 and each member collects it once in ten weeks.

Borrowing allows you to obtain money now and pay later with interest, so borrow only for important needs and only what you can repay. Loan apps and lenders that charge very high interest, or that harass borrowers, are dangerous. Read the terms before you agree.

Beware of investment scams. Ponzi schemes promise very high returns and pay old investors with new investors' money until they collapse. Warning signs: guaranteed high profits, pressure to join quickly and rewards for recruiting. Check that an investment company is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and ask a trusted adult first.

Good habits: save regularly, avoid unnecessary debt, keep records, give honestly and plan for the future.

Activity: Set a savings goal and compute how many weeks it takes if you save ₦500 each week.

lessons.title: Meaning and Scope of Social Studies
lessons.content:
# Meaning and Scope of Social Studies

Social Studies is the study of how people live together and how they relate to their environment. It draws ideas from history, geography, economics, government, sociology and religion so that we can understand ourselves, other people and our society and solve problems in them. The word social refers to people living together, and studies means learning about them systematically.

Social Studies aims to help learners become good citizens who know their rights and duties, respect other cultures, think for themselves, take responsibility and work for the progress of the community and the nation. It deals with topics such as the family, community, culture, government, rights, resources, population and national unity.

Example: The question Why are some Nigerian towns crowded while others are quiet? needs geography (location and land), economics (jobs) and history (how the towns developed). Social Studies helps us put all these together.

Activity: Write down three problems in your community that Social Studies could help you understand.
